1.1|Which of the following best describes the structural distinction between pre-colonial Nigerian societies?|Democratic versus autocratic systems|Centralized cephalous systems versus non-centralized acephalous systems|Industrialized versus agrarian economies|Nomadic pastoralist versus sedentary urban societies|Option B|Pre-colonial Nigerian societies are broadly classified into centralized cephalous kingdoms and empires, and non-centralized acephalous segmentary societies.
1.1|What is the defining characteristic of an acephalous society in the context of pre-colonial Nigerian history?|It possesses a single supreme monarch who holds absolute legislative power|It operates without a centralized, hierarchical ruling authority or single head of state|It relies exclusively on foreign administration for conflict resolution|It rejects all forms of religious and ancestral customs|Option B|Acephalous or non-centralized societies like the Igbo and Tiv operated without a single central ruling authority or monarch, instead relying on kinship and segmentary lineages.
1.1|Which of the following ethnic groups is classically categorized as a non-centralized or acephalous society in pre-colonial Nigeria?|Sokoto Caliphate|Oyo Empire|Igbo|Kanem-Bornu Empire|Option C|The Igbo people are well-documented examples of a pre-colonial acephalous society that utilized decentralized systems like age grades and lineage councils.
1.1|How was political authority primarily legitimized in centralized pre-colonial Nigerian kingdoms?|Through universal adult suffrage and periodic elections|Through sacred monarchy, ancestral lineage, and religious rituals|Through military occupation by foreign mercenaries|Through corporate board appointments and civil service exams|Option B|Centralized kingdoms derived their authority heavily from sacred monarchy, deep ancestral lineage ties, and sacred religious rituals that reinforced the ruler's divine right.
1.1|Which sociological term describes pre-colonial societies such as the Tiv that lacked centralized state machinery?|Segmentary societies|Feudal estates|Bicameral republics|Constitutional oligarchies|Option A|Segmentary societies consist of equivalent segments or clans that cooperate for defense and social order without a permanent centralized government.
1.1|What role did customary taboos and religious rituals play in pre-colonial administrative systems?|They were used solely for agricultural forecasting|They served as powerful mechanisms of social control and political compliance|They replaced the need for any form of economic trade|They were introduced solely by European colonial administrators|Option B|Customary taboos and religious rituals acted as spiritual and moral deterrents, enforcing laws and maintaining social order without a standing police force.
1.1|Which administrative feature was most prominent in cephalous pre-colonial systems like the Sokoto Caliphate or Oyo Empire?|Absolute absence of taxation|Hierarchical governance structures with delegated authorities like emirs or oba|Direct democratic voting by all citizens|Complete separation of religious and political institutions|Option B|Cephalous systems featured structured hierarchies with a supreme ruler delegating administrative powers to regional chiefs, emirs, or vassal kings.
1.1|In the study of Nigerian administrative history, what does the term cephalous denote?|The presence of a centralized head or monarch|The complete absence of a traditional leader|A nomadic lifestyle centered around cattle rearing|A system of governance based entirely on market trade unions|Option A|The term cephalous is derived from roots meaning having a head, representing centralized political systems with a distinct head of state.
1.1|Which of the following was a primary pillar of authority in non-centralized pre-colonial Nigerian communities?|A standing national army funded by income tax|Kinship ties, age-grade associations, and council of elders|Bureaucratic civil servants recruited through competitive examinations|A hereditary prime minister with executive veto power|Option B|Without a central monarch, non-centralized societies maintained governance and order through kinship networks, elder councils, and age grades.

7.1|Which of the following triad pillars formed the foundational core of Lord Lugard’s Indirect Rule system in Nigeria?|Native Authority, Native Courts, and Native Treasury|Legislative Council, Executive Council, and Provincial Courts|Customary Police, Warrant Chiefs, and Regional Assemblies|Emirs, Paramount Chiefs, and British Governors|Option A|Indirect Rule functioned through three main administrative pillars: the Native Authority (traditional rulers exercising power), Native Courts (for judicial administration), and Native Treasury (for local revenue collection and expenditure).

11.1|What fundamental institutional change occurred in Nigeria with the adoption of the 1979 Constitution regarding the executive branch?|Transition from a parliamentary Westminster system to an American-style executive presidential system|Merger of the judiciary and the legislature under a supreme legislative council|Establishment of a diarchy sharing power between military rulers and civilian technocrats|Devolution of all federal powers exclusively to regional governments|Option A|The 1979 Constitution marked a distinct structural departure from the British Westminster model by adopting the American Presidential model where executive powers are vested in a single individual.
11.1|Under the 1979 Presidential Constitution, how are the roles of Head of State and Head of Government structured?|Both positions are held concurrently and exclusively by the elected executive President|The Head of State is a ceremonial monarch while the Head of Government is the Prime Minister|The Senate President acts as Head of State while the Chief Justice serves as Head of Government|The roles are permanently rotated biennially among the governors of the federation|Option A|Unlike the Westminster system where the roles are split between a ceremonial Head of State and an executive Prime Minister, the executive President combines both offices.
11.1|Which constitutional doctrine underpins the structural arrangement of the 1979 Presidential Constitution among the Executive, National Assembly, and Judiciary?|Separation of powers and checks and balances|Democratic centralism and party supremacy|Unitary subordination of regional courts|Fused parliamentary sovereignty|Option A|The 1979 Constitution explicitly distributed governmental functions among three distinct arms—the Executive, Legislature, and Judiciary—to prevent tyranny and ensure institutional independence.
11.1|What was the primary constitutional purpose of introducing the Federal Character Principle in the 1979 Constitution?|To promote national unity and ensure balanced representation of diverse ethnic groups in public institutions|To grant exclusive economic resources to oil-producing minority communities in the Niger Delta|To establish a state religion recognized by all federal ministries and departments|To abolish all state civil service commissions in favor of a centralized bureaucracy|Option A|The Federal Character Principle was designed to reflect Nigeria's linguistic and cultural diversity, fostering a sense of belonging and preventing the dominance of any single group.
11.1|How did the 1979 Constitution attempt to curb regionalism and foster pan-Nigerian political parties?|By mandating strict national spread requirements for political party formation and leadership|By permitting only two state-funded political parties to contest national elections|By banning all political parties that had historical roots in the pre-independence era|By requiring political parties to register exclusively with traditional rulers in the North and South|Option A|To prevent ethnic polarization, the 1979 Constitution required political parties to demonstrate geographical spread and national character in their membership and executive composition.
11.1|Which branch of government under the 1979 Constitution is constitutionally empowered to enact federal laws?|The National Assembly|The Federal Executive Council|The Supreme Judicial Council|The Council of State|Option A|The National Assembly, consisting of the Senate and the House of Representatives, holds the primary legislative authority to make laws for the peace, order, and good government of the federation.
11.1|What distinguishes the position of the President under the 1979 Constitution from a Prime Minister in a Westminster system regarding legislative membership?|The President is not a member of the legislature, whereas a Prime Minister must be an elected parliamentarian|The President holds absolute veto power over legislative seats while the Prime Minister does not|The President can dissolve parliament at will without any constitutional checks|The President appoints all members of the opposition party directly into the cabinet|Option A|In the executive presidential system, the principle of separation of powers ensures that the President is independent of the legislature and does not sit in parliament.
11.1|Which organ of government is charged with the responsibility of interpreting the laws and resolving constitutional disputes under the 1979 Constitution?|The Judiciary|The National Security Council|The Federal Electoral Commission|The Civil Service Commission|Option A|The Judiciary holds the judicial power of the federation and acts as the final arbiter in interpreting the constitution and resolving disputes between other arms or tiers of government.

1.1|Which term best describes pre-colonial societies in Nigeria that lacked centralized authority structures and formal states?|Cephalous societies|Acephalous societies|Feudal monarchies|Theocratic caliphates|Option B|Acephalous or segmentary societies are characterized by the absence of a centralized political apparatus, contrasting with cephalous kingdoms and empires.
1.1|What primary source of legitimacy was most characteristic of centralized pre-colonial Nigerian states like kingdoms and empires?|Sacred monarchy and divine right|Universal adult suffrage and elections|Bureaucratic meritocracy and civil exams|Corporate capitalism and private property|Option A|Centralized pre-colonial systems heavily relied on sacred monarchy where rulers derived political authority from religious legitimacy and divine sanction.
1.1|In the context of pre-colonial Nigerian administrative history, what does a cephalous political system denote?|A society without a single head or central leader|A political structure featuring a centralized head or recognized leadership|A decentralized federation of independent village councils|A nomadic confederation without permanent territorial boundaries|Option B|Cephalous literally means having a head, representing centralized political entities like kingdoms, empires, and caliphates that possessed hierarchical administrative structures.

1.1|Which structural feature distinguishes a segmentary society from a centralized state in pre-colonial Nigeria?|The presence of a single hereditary monarch with absolute legislative powers|The division of society into equivalent, autonomous lineage segments without a single overarching government|The establishment of a permanent tax collection bureaucracy across all provinces|The creation of an industrial economy driven by wage labor|Option B|Segmentary societies consist of functionally equivalent, localized segments or clans that manage their affairs independently without a permanent centralized administrative machinery.

1.1|What primary characteristic distinguishes a cephalous pre-colonial Nigerian society from an acephalous one?|The presence of a structured, institutionalized central authority and hierarchical administration|A reliance exclusively on nomadic pastoralism rather than sedentary agriculture|The complete absence of any legal or moral codes of conduct|An economy based entirely on international maritime trade|Option A|Cephalous societies feature recognized hierarchical political structures and institutionalized central leadership, whereas acephalous societies are structured around kinship and segmentary lineages.

1.1|In pre-colonial centralized Nigerian systems, authority was frequently legitimized through which of the following mechanisms?|Universal adult suffrage and secret ballot elections|Sacred monarchy, ancestral lineage, and religious rituals|Strict constitutional separation of powers modeled after Western republics|Bureaucratic meritocracy based on written civil service examinations|Option B|Centralized systems relied heavily on traditional mechanisms such as sacred kingship, divine right, customary taboos, and ancestral lineage to maintain political legitimacy.
1.1|What sociological term is frequently used to describe acephalous societies where political power is distributed among various kinship segments?|Unitary state|Segmentary society|Plutocratic oligarchy|Totalitarian regime|Option B|Acephalous societies are often termed segmentary societies because power and social order are maintained through cooperating kinship segments and lineage groups rather than a central government.
1.1|How did customary taboos function within the administrative framework of pre-colonial Nigerian societies?|As formal written statutes enacted by a legislative assembly|As unwritten moral and religious constraints that reinforced social order and authority|As trade tariffs imposed on foreign merchants entering the kingdom|As military tactics used during inter-tribal warfare|Option B|Customary taboos served as powerful unwritten social controls backed by religious sanctions, helping to maintain order and reinforce the legitimacy of traditional authority.

1.1|What role did religious rituals play in the exercise of authority across pre-colonial Nigerian communities?|They were viewed as entirely separate from political governance and statecraft.|They provided ideological backing and spiritual sanctity to political office holders.|They served as the primary legal code for resolving commercial contract disputes.|They were used exclusively by foreign traders to conduct religious ceremonies.|Option B|Religious rituals were deeply intertwined with political administration, providing the spiritual validation and sacred aura necessary for rulers to command obedience.

1.1|In pre-colonial centralized polities, what was a primary source of political legitimacy and authority for the monarch?|Sacred kingship rooted in religious rituals and ancestral lineage|Popular democratic elections held at regular constitutional intervals|Universal adult suffrage supervised by independent civil service commissions|Foreign recognition by neighboring international treaties and charters|Option A|Authority in centralized systems was deeply tied to sacred monarchy, where rulers derived legitimacy through divine sanction, rituals, and ancestral links.
1.1|Which Nigerian societies are classic examples of non-centralized or acephalous pre-colonial administrative systems?|The Igbo and Tiv societies|The Oyo Empire and the Sokoto Caliphate|The Kanem-Borno Empire and the Benin Kingdom|The Jukun Kingdom and the Igala Monarchy|Option A|The Igbo and Tiv are textbook examples of segmentary, acephalous societies that managed administration through kinship, councils of elders, and age-grades.
1.1|What role did customary taboos play in the administrative governance of pre-colonial Nigerian communities?|They served as powerful social control mechanisms that regulated behavior and reinforced authority|They were written legal codes enforced by professional judicial magistrates|They functioned exclusively as economic taxes imposed on foreign traders|They were temporary rules discarded during periods of agricultural harvest|Option A|Customary taboos acted as spiritual and moral deterrents that maintained social order and bolstered political and religious authority.
1.1|How was political administration primarily coordinated in traditional Igbo society prior to European colonization?|Through decentralized lineage heads, village assemblies, and age-grade associations|Through absolute decrees issued by an elected paramount sovereign|Through a centralized standing army controlled by a hereditary king|Through a bureaucratic network of provincial tax collectors appointed from a capital city|Option A|Igbo administration was famously decentralized, utilizing kindred groups, open-forum village assemblies (Oha-na-eze), and age-grades for collective decision-making.
1.1|Which of the following institutions was central to maintaining social cohesion and governance in Tiv pre-colonial society?|Kinship ties and genealogical segmentary lineages|A centralized royal court with appointed ministers of state|A standing feudal cavalry commanded by regional warlords|A legislative parliament with elected representatives from all districts|Option A|Tiv society was organized around segmentary lineages linked through genealogy, where authority was exercised by lineage elders.
1.1|What distinguishes the basis of authority in traditional African administrative systems from modern legal-rational authority?|Reliance on sacred monarchy, tradition, and custom rather than written constitutional laws|Complete dependence on foreign legal codes imported from overseas empires|Absence of any formal norms or expectations governing social behavior|Purely economic determination of leadership based on individual monetary wealth|Option A|Pre-colonial authority relied heavily on traditional and charismatic legitimacy, including custom, sacred monarchy, and rituals, unlike modern bureaucratic systems.
1.1|Why is the study of pre-colonial administrative history crucial for understanding modern Nigerian public administration?|It provides the foundational context of indigenous governance values upon which modern systems were superimposed|It proves that pre-colonial societies lacked any form of organized social order or governance|It demonstrates that western administrative models were adopted without any indigenous resistance|It focuses exclusively on the economic trade routes of the trans-Saharan era without political relevance|Option A|Understanding pre-colonial structures explains the historical evolution, complexities, and cultural context of Nigeria's contemporary administrative framework.
4.1|Which fundamental political concept best describes the pre-colonial traditional administrative system of the Igbo as captured by the phrase Igbo Enwe Eze|Absolute monarchy with centralized royal authority|Segmentary democracy characterized by non-hierarchical governance|Feudal oligarchy controlled by a powerful landed aristocracy|Military dictatorship based on conquest and expansionism|Option B|The Igbo political system is famously described as segmentary democracy because authority was decentralized, non-hierarchical, and based on direct consensus rather than single-ruler monarchy.
4.1|What is the primary socio-political significance of the Umunna in traditional Igbo administration|It represents the supreme council of elders responsible for final judicial verdicts|It functions as the royal cabinet appointed directly by the traditional monarch|It serves as the extended family lineage group forming the basic building block of societal organization|It operates exclusively as a secret society for spiritual rituals and rain-making|Option C|The Umunna is the foundational extended family lineage group in Igbo society that fosters communal solidarity, social security, and localized conflict resolution.
4.1|In the traditional Igbo administrative structure, what is the primary role of the Okpara|Serving as the commander-in-chief of the village war council and defense forces|Holding the sacred Ofo staff as the oldest male representative and spiritual head of the lineage|Acting as the paramount king who collects taxes and levies on behalf of the community|Functioning as the chief merchant who regulates all inter-ethnic trade and commerce|Option B|The Okpara is the head of the family lineage who holds the sacred Ofo staff symbolizing truth, authority, and ancestral connection.
4.1|Who constitutes the membership of the Oha-na-Eze assembly in traditional Igbo political organization|Only the wealthy titleholders of the Ozo society|Exclusively female elders and priestesses of the earth goddess|All adult males of the village community|Delegates appointed by neighboring kingdoms through diplomacy|Option C|The Oha-na-Eze is the comprehensive village assembly comprising all adult males, embodying participatory democracy where consensus is sought on public matters.
4.1|What distinguishes the Ndichie institution within the traditional governance framework of Igbo land|They are hereditary prime ministers with absolute veto power over assembly decisions|They form the council of elders whose accumulated wisdom guides community deliberations and dispute settlements|They operate as youth vigilantes responsible for night patrols and manual labor|They function as tax collectors representing foreign colonial interests|Option B|The Ndichie are respected elders who utilize their wisdom and experience to guide deliberations and resolve complex community disputes.
4.1|How is membership into the Ozo or Nze society earned or attained in traditional Igbo society|Through hereditary succession from father to firstborn son regardless of merit|Through wealth accumulation, personal integrity, high moral standing, and initiation rites|Through appointment by colonial district officers based on literacy and obedience|Through victory in annual wrestling competitions and military duels|Option B|The Ozo/Nze title society is an esteemed institution achieved through personal integrity, wealth, and moral character, reflecting an open and achievement-based stratified status.
4.1|What is the primary functional responsibility of the Age Grades known as Uke or Ogbo in Igbo administration|Performing priestly sacrifices to appease ancestral spirits during planting seasons|Executing public works, maintaining community infrastructure, and enforcing laws and assembly decisions|Conducting foreign policy negotiations and treaty-making with distant empires|Serving as the primary judiciary that interprets customary laws in capital offenses|Option B|Age grades (Uke or Ogbo) act as the operational arm of the community, mobilized for public works, sanitation, communal labor, and law enforcement.
4.1|What unique administrative and socio-political role does the Umuada perform in traditional Igbo society|They serve as the daughters of the lineage who intervene effectively to resolve domestic disputes and mediate conflicts|They function as absolute monarchs who rule over market women associations|They act as combat units deployed exclusively for offensive territorial expansion wars|They operate as religious recluses forbidden from participating in public meetings|Option A|The Umuada (assembly of married and unmarried daughters of the lineage) wields significant moral and political authority, often acting as effective peace-makers and mediators in family conflicts.
4.1|Which statement best characterizes the decision-making process inherent in the traditional Igbo political system|Decisions are imposed top-down through royal decrees issued by the paramount ruler|Policies are determined through majority voting backed by police coercion and imprisonment|Governance relies on prolonged deliberations aiming at absolute consensus among participants|Laws are enacted secretly by ritual priests without public consultation or debate|Option C|Traditional Igbo governance relies heavily on direct consensus democracy where issues are discussed extensively until a general agreement is reached.
4.1|Why is the pre-colonial Igbo administrative system frequently categorized by political scientists as acephalous|Because it possessed a massive head tax administrative apparatus spread across provinces|Because it operated without a centralized monarch, paramount ruler, or single head of state|Because political power was concentrated solely in the hands of the coastal merchant princes|Because governance was dictated from distant administrative capitals in foreign lands|Option B|Acephalous literally means headless, denoting stateless societies that function efficiently without a centralized king or hierarchical royal government.

7.1|The Richard Constitution of 1946 is historically significant for introducing which of the following administrative features?|A strict unitary system that abolished all forms of local tribal governance|The formal division of the country into three distinct administrative regions|Universal adult suffrage for all citizens residing in Lagos and Calabar|The complete independence of the Nigerian civil service from British control|Option B|Sir Arthur Richards' constitution of 1946 laid the structural foundation for regionalism by dividing Nigeria into Northern, Western, and Eastern regions.

7.1|What major structural change was formally introduced by the Lyttelton Constitution of 1954?|The abolition of regional legislatures in favor of a single national assembly|The establishment of formal federalism alongside the creation of regional civil services|The introduction of the very first elective principle in British West Africa|The replacement of traditional rulers with democratically elected prime ministers|Option C|The Lyttelton Constitution of 1954 firmly established a federal system of government and decentralized power by creating distinct regional civil services.

1.1|How are acephalous or non-centralized pre-colonial Nigerian societies primarily characterized regarding political authority?|Power is concentrated within a single hereditary monarch who holds absolute executive powers|Political authority is dispersed across segmentary lineages, age-grades, and kinship groups without a single overarching ruler|Governance is strictly dictated by external colonial military overlords|Administrative decisions are exclusively handled by a standing professional judiciary|Option B|Acephalous or non-centralized societies, such as the Igbo and Tiv, diffused political authority among segmentary lineages and kin groups rather than concentrating it in a single ruler.
1.1|Which of the following ethnic groups is classically categorized as a non-centralized or acephalous pre-colonial society in Nigeria?|The Sokoto Caliphate|The Oyo Empire|The Igbo society|The Benin Kingdom|Option C|The traditional Igbo society is widely studied as a classic example of an acephalous or segmentary pre-colonial administrative system in Nigeria.
1.1|What fundamental role did sacred monarchy play in centralized pre-colonial Nigerian administrations?|It served purely as a ceremonial title with zero influence over political or judicial decisions|It legitimized political rule by blending spiritual authority with temporal governance to ensure social cohesion|It mandated the total separation of religious practices from state administrative machinery|It functioned strictly as an economic cooperative body for agricultural trade|Option B|Sacred monarchy intertwined spiritual and temporal authority, using religious sanctity to legitimize the ruler's power and maintain social order.
1.1|In pre-colonial Tiv society, what served as a primary structural basis for social and political organization?|Ancestral lineage and kinship ties|A centralized divine kingship with absolute legislative power|A standing bureaucratic civil service with salaried bureaucrats|A feudal system based on manorial land ownership|Option A|Tiv society, like other acephalous systems, organized its social and political life primarily around ancestral lineage and kinship connections.
1.1|Which mechanism was frequently utilized in pre-colonial societies to enforce moral conduct and political compliance without a formal police force?|Customary taboos and religious rituals|International maritime law codes|Written statutory penal codes enacted by elected parliaments|Standing professional mercenary armies garrisoned in every village|Option A|Customary taboos and religious rituals acted as powerful internal social controls that ensured conformity and law enforcement in pre-colonial communities.
1.1|What distinguishes a cephalous administrative structure from an acephalous one in Nigerian history?|Cephalous systems feature a centralized head or recognized political authority, whereas acephalous systems lack a single central ruler|Cephalous systems rely on written constitutions, while acephalous systems use oral traditions exclusively|Cephalous systems are exclusively democratic, while acephalous systems are strictly autocratic|Cephalous systems exist only in coastal regions, while acephalous systems are confined to deserts|Option A|The term cephalous comes from the Greek root for head, denoting societies with a centralized political head or monarch, unlike acephalous headless societies.
1.1|Which administrative feature was common to large pre-colonial Nigerian formations like the Sokoto Caliphate and the Oyo Empire?|Bureaucratic delegation of power through appointed officials or vassal chiefs|Complete absence of taxation or tribute systems|Universal adult suffrage for all residents regardless of status|Absolute political equality among all adult male and female citizens|Option A|Centralized empires and caliphates managed extensive territories by delegating administrative responsibilities through hierarchies of appointed officials and vassal rulers.
1.1|How did customary laws maintain stability within pre-colonial Nigerian administrative systems?|Through rigid enforcement backed by unwritten shared values, ancestral precedents, and community consensus|Through daily amendments passed by multi-party legislative assemblies|Through binding judicial precedents published in official state gazettes|Through foreign legal frameworks imported from neighboring continents|Option A|Customary laws derived their binding force from shared traditions, ancestral heritage, and community consensus rather than codified statutory enactments.
1.1|Which factor best explains the resilience of acephalous political structures during the pre-colonial era?|Their decentralized segmentary nature made them adaptable and resistant to total collapse from the removal of a single leader|Their possession of advanced gunpowder weaponry deterred external invasions|Their complete isolation from all trade networks prevented external political interference|Their centralized economic planning board monopolized all regional resources|Option A|Because authority in acephalous societies was distributed across various kinship and lineage segments, the system could easily withstand local disruptions without collapsing.
11.1|What foundational structural shift characterized Nigeria's transition from the First Republic to the 1979 Presidential Constitution?|Adoption of a parliamentary system modeled strictly after the British Westminster model|Introduction of a dual executive where the Head of State and Head of Government are separate offices|Concentration of all legislative and judicial powers within the executive branch|Consolidation of the roles of Head of State and Head of Government into a single elected President|Option D|The 1979 Constitution abandoned the Westminster parliamentary model in favor of the American presidential system, merging the offices of Head of State and Head of Government.
11.1|Which constitutional doctrine was fundamentally introduced in the 1979 Constitution to prevent the arbitrary concentration of power among the branches of government?|The principle of collective ministerial responsibility|The doctrine of separation of powers among the Executive, National Assembly, and Judiciary|The system of parliamentary supremacy over regional laws|The policy of bureaucratic centralization under a unitary framework|Option B|The 1979 Constitution strictly demarcated governance into three independent arms—the Executive, National Assembly, and Judiciary—emulating the American separation of powers model.
11.1|What was the primary constitutional purpose behind the introduction of the Federal Character Principle in the 1979 Nigerian Constitution?|To ensure absolute financial autonomy for state and local government treasuries|To eliminate political parties that failed to secure a majority in the federal legislature|To promote national unity and command national loyalty by preventing the dominance of any single ethnic group in governance|To streamline the civil service recruitment process purely on academic merit without regional considerations|Option C|The Federal Character Principle was designed to reflect the linguistic and ethnic diversity of Nigeria in government positions, fostering a sense of belonging and national integration.
11.1|In the context of the 1979 Presidential Constitution, how did the electoral requirements for political parties differ fundamentally from previous eras?|Parties were required to demonstrate a strict national spread in both membership and geographical support base rather than relying purely on regional strongholds|Parties were permitted to operate solely within their regional boundaries provided they won a plurality of local council seats|Parties had to be directly funded and supervised by traditional ruling councils in each geopolitical zone|Parties were restricted from fielding presidential candidates unless they won every state legislature election|Option A|To prevent regional fragmentation, the 1979 Constitution mandated that political parties exhibit a broad national spread, discouraging regionally or ethnically isolated factions.
11.1|Which of the following best describes the structural design of the legislature established under the 1979 Nigerian Constitution?|A unicameral legislature modeled after traditional council assemblies|A bicameral National Assembly consisting of a Senate and a House of Representatives|A tripartite parliament composed of regional delegates and federal ministers|A unicameral assembly exclusively representing regional state governors|Option B|The 1979 Constitution established a bicameral National Assembly comprising the Senate and the House of Representatives to ensure balanced federal representation.
11.1|How did the relationship between the executive branch and the legislature under the 1979 Presidential Constitution differ from the Westminster system?|Executive ministers were concurrently required to maintain active membership as elected members of the national parliament|The executive branch was fully subordinate to legislative votes of no confidence at any given time|Executive cabinet members were appointed from outside the legislature, maintaining a strict institutional division between law-makers and policy-implementers|The President possessed the absolute authority to dissolve the parliament at will without constitutional checks|Option C|Under the presidential system, ministers (commissioners) cannot be members of the legislature, thereby enforcing a strict institutional separation between the executive and legislative branches.
11.1|What core philosophy underpinned the adoption of the American Executive Presidential model for Nigeria in 1979?|The belief that a powerful single executive could effectively bridge ethnic divides and provide strong, decisive national leadership|The goal of restoring colonial administrative structures to enhance bureaucratic efficiency|The desire to subordinate the judiciary completely to executive policy directives|The intention to establish a unitary state with absolute centralization of power in Lagos|Option A|Framers of the 1979 Constitution believed an executive president with a national mandate would serve as a unifying symbol above regional divisions.
11.1|Under the 1979 Constitution, what was the constitutional status of the Judiciary relative to the executive and legislative arms?|It functioned as an advisory committee reporting directly to the executive cabinet|It served as an independent third branch of government empowered with powers of judicial review|It was subordinate to legislative decrees passed by a two-thirds majority in parliament|It operated solely as a mechanism for enforcing customary laws within local administrative districts|Option B|The 1979 Constitution entrenched the judiciary as an independent arm of government capable of checking executive and legislative excesses through judicial review.
11.1|Which challenge was the Federal Character Principle specifically intended to mitigate within the Nigerian public administration system?|Frequent military coups d'état caused by budgetary deficits in regional treasuries|Perceptions of ethnic marginalization and exclusion in public service appointments and federal institutions|Disputes over the collection and distribution of petroleum profit taxes among oil-producing states|Inefficiencies caused by the duplication of ministries between federal and state levels|Option B|The principle was instituted to address deep-seated fears of domination by certain groups by ensuring equitable representation of all states in public institutions.
11.1|What distinctive attribute separated the 1979 Nigerian presidential executive from the parliamentary prime minister of the First Republic?|The 1979 President was accountable to parliament through weekly question-and-answer sessions|The 1979 President combined the ceremonial duties of Head of State with the executive powers of Head of Government|The 1979 President shared executive authority equally with a co-elected Prime Minister|The 1979 President held office indefinitely subject to the approval of the Council of State|Option B|Unlike the parliamentary system where executive power was split between a ceremonial Head of State and an executive Prime Minister, the 1979 President held both roles concurrently.
13.1|Which key structural change was introduced by the nationwide local government reform of 1976 in Nigeria?|Establishment of a multi-tiered administrative structure across all regions|Adoption of a uniform single-tier local government system nationwide|Delegation of exclusive tax-collection powers to traditional rulers|Abolition of local government councils as an autonomous tier of governance|Option B|The 1976 reform dismantled fragmented colonial structures to establish a uniform single-tier system across the entire federation.
13.1|What status was formally conferred upon local governments by the 1976 local government reform?|A subordinate regional department under state ministries|An autonomous fourth tier of the federation|The third tier of government within the federal structure|A private corporate entity managed by traditional rulers|Option C|The 1976 reform officially recognized local government as the third tier of government, distinct from federal and state structures.
13.1|How did the 1976 reform fundamentally alter the administrative role of traditional rulers in local governance?|By appointing traditional rulers as the sole executive chairmen of local councils|By completely abolishing traditional institutions nationwide|By insulating traditional rulers and restricting them to advisory councils|By granting traditional rulers veto power over council financial budgets|Option C|Traditional rulers were intentionally insulated from active partisan politics and executive duties by restricting them to advisory councils.
13.1|What financial mechanism was introduced by the 1976 reform to ensure financial viability for local governments?|Statutory revenue allocation directly from the Federation Account|Collection of international grants from foreign donor agencies|Full reliance on local market levies without central government transfers|Discretionary loans issued exclusively by regional governors|Option A|The reform guaranteed financial sustainability by introducing statutory revenue allocations from the Federation Account.
13.1|Which administrative milestone was a primary focus of the Dasuki Committee of 1984 regarding local government?|Reorganizing the judiciary to handle local civil disputes exclusively|Reviewing local government structure and administrative efficiency|Privatizing all public utilities operated by local authorities|Transferring local government oversight to international monitors|Option B|The Dasuki Committee of 1984 was established to review the structure, funding, and general performance of local government administration in Nigeria.
13.1|What significant executive leadership position was introduced during the Babangida reforms of 1988 following earlier reviews?|Appointed Military Administrator for each local government area|Executive Chairman elected to lead local government administration|State Commissioner for Local Affairs acting as executive head|Permanent Secretary heading the local council secretariat|Option B|The 1988 reforms under Babangida introduced the position of Executive Chairman to strengthen political leadership and administrative accountability at the grassroots.
13.1|Which change characterized the evolution of revenue transfers to local governments following the mid-1980s reforms?|Direct revenue transfers to minimize state-level bureaucratic delays|Routing all funds through traditional council treasuries|Eliminating federal allocations in favor of direct foreign aid|Abolishing all forms of statutory grants to local authorities|Option A|Subsequent reforms introduced direct revenue transfers to local councils to enhance financial autonomy and reduce arbitrary state interference.
13.1|What was the major administrative defect of pre-1976 local administration that the uniform single-tier reform sought to correct?|Excessive federal oversight that stifled grassroots initiatives|Fragmented, multi-tiered, and non-uniform systems across different regions|Complete lack of any traditional authority involvement|Absence of any taxation powers for local communities|Option B|Before 1976, Nigeria suffered from fragmented and varied local administration systems across regions, prompting the push for a uniform structure.
13.1|Why were traditional rulers insulated from executive council responsibilities in the 1976 reform?|To prevent conflicts between modern bureaucratic authority and traditional monarchy|To strip them of all cultural recognition and influence in society|To transfer royal lands directly to the federal government|To force them to relocate to urban administrative headquarters|Option A|Insulation protected traditional rulers from partisan politics and minimized friction between elected modern administrators and traditional leaders.
13.1|The integration of local governments as the third tier of government in 1976 primarily aimed to achieve which objective?|Bring government closer to the grassroots and stimulate national development|Centralize all development planning exclusively in the federal capital|Merge local administration completely with state civil service departments|Replace state governments with powerful municipal councils|Option A|Recognizing local government as the third tier was designed to devolve power, bring governance closer to the grassroots, and drive development.

3.1|How many elite military commanders made up the famous Eso Ikoyi war council protecting the frontiers of the empire?|Fifty commanders|Seventy commanders|One hundred commanders|Forty commanders|Option B|The Eso Ikoyi comprised a specialized corps of seventy valiant military commanders tasked with defending the territorial integrity of the empire.
3.1|What unique institutional requirement was imposed on the Aare Ona Kakanfo as the supreme military commander of the Oyo army?|Must establish permanent residence within the capital palace|Must retire from military service after three consecutive victories|Must emerge victorious in every military campaign or face death by ritual suicide|Must hold membership in the Ogboni society prior to appointment|Option C|The Aare Ona Kakanfo was bound by tradition to win all military expeditions or commit suicide if defeated on the battlefield.

3.1|Which administrative mechanism was primarily responsible for preventing absolute autocracy and monarchical tyranny in the Oyo Empire?|A rigorous system of checks and balances involving the Oyo Mesi and the Ogboni|Direct democratic elections held annually across all provincial districts|Absolute military dominance by the provincial governors over the central palace|External oversight by neighboring allied kingdoms|Option A|The system of checks and balances, spearheaded by the Oyo Mesi and moderated by the Ogboni, effectively prevented the Alaafin from exercising absolute unchecked power.

8.1|What direct consequence did British colonial rule have on indigenous governance mechanisms within traditional institutions?|Customary checks and balances were severely eroded|Traditional legislative councils were expanded and democratized|Indigenous taxation systems were completely abolished in favor of voluntary donations|The power of District Officers was subordinated to local village councils|Option A|The imposition of British rule undermined native governance by eroding customary checks and balances that previously held leaders accountable.
8.1|To whom were traditional chiefs primarily required to report under the administrative structure established by the British?|District Officers and Residents|Village elders and age-grade associations|Traditional council assemblies and local town unions|Elected representatives of the provincial parliament|Option A|Traditional chiefs reported directly to colonial administrative officers like District Officers and Residents rather than to their local citizens.

1.1|In pre-colonial centralized Nigerian systems, what primary source of legitimacy did rulers rely on to reinforce their political power and social control?|Popular democratic elections|Secular written constitutions|Sacred monarchy and divine right|Foreign military intervention|Option C|Centralized monarchies drew immense authority from sacred traditions, viewing the ruler as divinely appointed or closely tied to ancestral deities.
1.1|How did non-centralized (acephalous) societies like the pre-colonial Igbo and Tiv primarily maintain social order and administrative cohesion?|Through standing national armies and police forces|Through ancestral lineage, kinship ties, and age-grades|Through strict taxation and centralized bureaucratic offices|Through a single supreme monarch exercising absolute law|Option B|In the absence of a central state apparatus, acephalous societies maintained order through decentralized networks based on kinship, lineages, and communal age-grades.
1.1|Which historical example best represents a centralized (cephalous) pre-colonial administrative system in Nigeria?|The Igbo village assembly|The Tiv lineage council|The Sokoto Caliphate|The nomadic pastoralist union|Option C|The Sokoto Caliphate was a highly organized, centralized imperial administrative system featuring emirs, a vizier, and systematic taxation.
1.1|What role did customary taboos and religious rituals play within pre-colonial Nigerian administrative systems?|They were used exclusively for agricultural planning without political impact|They served as informal mechanisms of social control and compliance|They were modern legal codes introduced by European colonizers|They replaced traditional judicial courts completely|Option D|Taboos and rituals acted as powerful moral and spiritual checks that enforced customary laws and ensured behavioral compliance without formal police.
1.1|Which of the following describes a key structural difference between a centralized empire and a segmentary acephalous society in pre-colonial Nigeria?|Centralized societies lacked any form of leadership while acephalous societies had kings|Centralized systems concentrated power in a hierarchical leadership whereas acephalous systems dispersed authority horizontally|Acephalous societies practiced industrial taxation while centralized systems did not|Centralized systems relied entirely on democratic voting while acephalous societies used hereditary monarchies|Option B|Centralized states concentrated authority in a hierarchical governing structure, whereas acephalous societies distributed power across decentralized kinship groups and autonomous communities.
1.1|What administrative feature was common to pre-colonial Nigerian systems regardless of whether they were centralized or non-centralized?|Reliance on written bureaucratic statutes|Absolute subordination to external colonial powers|Utilization of indigenous socio-cultural institutions for governance|Complete absence of any form of judicial settlement|Option C|Both political types effectively utilized deeply rooted indigenous institutions like councils of elders, family heads, and religious customs to manage communal affairs.
1.1|In the context of pre-colonial administration, how was authority traditionally transmitted and legitimized within ancestral lineage structures?|Through competitive public civil service examinations|Through hereditary descent and seniority within the clan|Through appointment by a central federal legislature|Through direct appointment by foreign trading companies|Option B|Authority within ancestral lineage frameworks was typically vested in elders and family heads whose legitimacy derived from seniority and ancestral connection.
1.1|Which classification accurately categorizes the pre-colonial administrative structures of both the Yoruba kingdoms and the Hausa city-states?|Acephalous and egalitarian systems|Segmentary and stateless tribal units|Centralized and cephalous political systems|Purely nomadic confederations|Option C|Both the Yoruba kingdoms and Hausa city-states possessed well-defined, centralized political structures featuring kings, court officials, and territorial administration.
4.1|Which fundamental political concept best describes the pre-colonial traditional administrative system of Igbo land summarized by the phrase Igbo Enwe Eze|Absolute monarchical autocracy|Centralized feudal oligarchy|Segmentary and direct consensus democracy|Theocratic priestly dictatorship|Option C|Igbo Enwe Eze translates to the concept that the Igbos have no king, operating instead through a non-hierarchical, segmentary system driven by direct consensus.
4.1|What primary socio-political role does the Umunna play within the traditional Igbo administrative structure|Serving as the supreme royal court with exclusive appellate jurisdiction over all provinces|Acting as the extended family lineage unit that forms the foundational bedrock of local governance|Functioning exclusively as a commercial cartel regulating cross-border trade tariffs|Operating as a standing military mercenary force responsible for territorial expansion|Option B|The Umunna represents the extended family lineage group which serves as the primary socio-political building block and safety net in traditional Igbo society.
4.1|What sacred symbol of authority and truth does the Okpara hold as the head of the Umunna lineage|The royal beaded crown and golden scepter|The ancestral Ofo staff of authority|The ceremonial bronze sword of execution|The sacred iron staff of the supreme oracle|Option C|The Okpara holds the Ofo staff, which is revered as a sacred symbol of truth, authority, and ancestral connection in Igbo lineage governance.
4.1|Who constitutes the membership of the Oha-na-eze assembly in traditional Igbo administration|Only the hereditary royal family members and court scribes|All adult male citizens of the village community|Exclusively wealthy titleholders of the Ozo society|Only the oldest female elders of the Umuada group|Option B|The Oha-na-eze is the broad village assembly comprising all adult males who gather to deliberate and reach consensus on community matters.
4.1|What is the primary function of the Age Grades known as Uke or Ogbo within the traditional Igbo administrative framework|Enacting supreme laws and interpreting complex metaphysical religious dogmas|Executing public works, maintaining community infrastructure, and enforcing law and order|Serving as the sole hereditary judicial tribunal for land boundary disputes|Collecting external taxes on behalf of neighboring centralized kingdoms|Option B|Age grades are organized groups of youth and adults assigned key communal responsibilities like public works, sanitation, and law enforcement.
4.1|What key societal value does the acquisition of the Ozo or Nze title signify in traditional Igbo communities|Military conquest and tactical battlefield prowess|Purity of lineage and hereditary divine right to rule|Personal integrity wealth and high moral standing|Absolute spiritual priesthood over the earth deity|Option C|The Ozo or Nze title society is attained by individuals of proven integrity, wealth, and high moral standing to participate actively in leadership.
4.1|What distinct socio-political role do the Umuada perform within their natal villages during disputes and community affairs|Acting as a powerful female lineage assembly that mediates conflicts and exerts moral pressure|Serving as exclusive priestesses of the village war shrine|Functioning as trade representatives in inter-ethnic commodity markets|Compiling written genealogies of the extended kinship groups|Option A|The Umuada functions as a collective assembly of daughters born into the lineage who act as powerful neutral mediators and moral arbiters during crises.
4.1|How are major community decisions traditionally reached within the acephalous political framework of Igbo land|Through imperial decrees issued by a supreme paramount ruler|Through direct consensus building among adult citizens in public assemblies|Through majority voting with strict disenfranchisement of commoners|Through divine pronouncements delivered exclusively by foreign mercenaries|Option B|Acephalous democracy in Igbo land relies heavily on dialogue and direct consensus building rather than authoritarian decrees or majority rule.
4.1|Which group constitutes the Ndichie institution within the traditional administrative layout of Igbo communities|The council of elders and titled patriarchs who advise on governance|The secret guild of blacksmiths and metalworkers|The association of young unmarried maidens responsible for festival planning|The visiting merchants from neighboring centralized empires|Option A|The Ndichie are the respected council of elders whose accumulated wisdom and community experience guide political and judicial deliberations.
4.1|Why is pre-colonial Igbo administration frequently classified by political scientists as acephalous|Because it possessed a rigid hierarchy of hereditary provincial kings|Because it operated successfully without a centralized king or hierarchical supreme authority|Because power was concentrated solely in the hands of a single religious oracle|Because governance was entirely imported from foreign colonial administrators|Option B|Acephalous literally means headless, reflecting the stateless, non-hierarchical, and decentralized nature of traditional Igbo governance without a central monarch.
2.1|Which major economic shift characterized the transition of Niger Delta city-states such as Bonny and Kalabari during the 19th century?|Shift from pastoral nomadism to intensive agrarian farming|Transition from the transatlantic slave trade to palm oil legitimate commerce|Shift from maritime trading monopolies to landlocked feudalism|Transition from industrial manufacturing to subsistence gathering|Option B|The Niger Delta city-states successfully transitioned their economic foundation from the transatlantic slave trade to palm oil legitimate commerce following abolition movements.
2.1|What was the primary socio-political function of secret societies like the Ekpe within the coastal city-states?|Enforcing contracts and maintaining public order|Regulating maritime weather patterns and fishing seasons|Selecting foreign trade partners from European nations|Conducting military campaigns against inland empires|Option A|Secret societies such as Ekpe acted as institutional mechanisms for enforcing commercial contracts and ensuring public order within the decentralized city-states.
2.1|How was authority structured within the traditional Canoe House System of the Niger Delta?|Absolute centralized control by a single hereditary monarch|Autocratic rule dictated by visiting European merchants|Corporate trading and governance led by merchant chiefs known as Amanyanabo|Democratic election of leaders by all adult male citizens|Option C|The Canoe House System was a corporate socio-economic and political organization headed by merchant chiefs and the Amanyanabo, functioning as both a trading unit and a governing body.
2.1|Which of the following coastal groups is explicitly recognized among the city-states that evolved administrative systems in the Niger Delta?|Itsekiri|Hausa-Fulani|Kanuri|Tiv|Option A|The Itsekiri are identified alongside Bonny, Nembe, and Kalabari as key coastal kingdoms that developed structured administrative systems in Southern Nigeria.
2.1|In the context of the Canoe House System, what does the term Wari primarily refer to?|A sacred religious shrine used for coronation rituals|The local currency used for palm oil transactions|A traditional war canoe or house organization functioning as a corporate unit|An architectural fortress built for protection against colonial invasion|Option C|Wari refers to the house or canoe organization, which served as a corporate socio-economic institution managing trade fleets and governance.
2.1|What primary role did the Amanyanabo play within the political framework of the coastal kingdoms?|Chief executive or king heading the administration and canoe houses|Foreign diplomat representing the kingdom in Europe|Head priest responsible for agricultural fertility rituals|Commander of the inland cavalry forces|Option A|The Amanyanabo served as the ruler or king who oversaw the governance structure and coordinated the activities of the powerful merchant chiefs.
2.1|Why did the transition from the slave trade to legitimate commerce require new enforcement mechanisms like the Ekpe society?|European merchants refused to use written contracts without native security|The shift to bulk commodity trading required reliable local institutions to guarantee credit and debt settlement|The abolition of slavery led to immediate total civil anarchy requiring military rule|Traditional chieftaincy titles were entirely abolished by colonial fiat|Option B|Legitimate commerce in palm oil involved extensive credit and deferred payments, necessitating powerful indigenous institutions like Ekpe to enforce commercial agreements.
2.1|Which administrative feature best distinguished the Niger Delta city-states from large centralized empires like the Sokoto Caliphate?|Total absence of any hierarchical leadership structure|Reliance on corporate merchant households rather than vast territorial bureaucracies|Complete subordination to foreign colonial governors from inception|Exclusive focus on subsistence agriculture over external trade|Option B|Unlike vast territorial empires, the Niger Delta city-states operated through decentralized corporate merchant households and canoe houses tailored to maritime commerce.
2.1|The shift toward legitimate commerce in the Niger Delta was primarily driven by which historical development?|The industrial revolution in Europe creating high demand for machine lubricants|The discovery of vast gold reserves in the hinterlands of Southern Nigeria|The complete unification of all coastal kingdoms under one monarch|The invention of steam-powered locomotives requiring coal fuel|Option A|The European Industrial Revolution created a massive demand for vegetable oils like palm oil to lubricate machinery, driving the economic shift in the region.
2.1|Which of the following city-states is specifically associated with the administrative developments of the Niger Delta alongside Bonny and Kalabari?|Nembe|Kano|Oyo|Zaria|Option A|Nembe is one of the prominent Niger Delta city-states that participated in the transition to legitimate commerce and developed the Canoe House administrative framework.
10.1|What fundamental constitutional change was introduced in Nigeria on October 1 1963 regarding the Head of State?|The British monarch was replaced by a ceremonial Nigerian President|Executive powers were transferred entirely to a military governorate|The office of the Prime Minister was abolished in favor of a US-style presidency|Nigeria formally rejoined the British Commonwealth as a dominion territory|Option A|The 1963 Republican Constitution severed the final constitutional ties with the British monarchy, making Dr. Nnamdi Azikiwe a ceremonial President of Nigeria.
10.1|Which judicial body replaced the London Privy Council as Nigeria's highest court of appeal under the 1963 Republican Constitution?|The Supreme Court of Nigeria|The West African Court of Appeal|The Federal Court of Arbitration|The International Court of Justice at The Hague|Option A|The 1963 Constitution localized the apex of judicial authority by establishing the Supreme Court of Nigeria as the ultimate court of appeal, replacing the London Privy Council.
10.1|Dr. Nnamdi Azikiwe assumed which specific role following the implementation of the 1963 Republican Constitution?|Ceremonial Nigerian Head of State|Executive Prime Minister and Commander-in-Chief|Governor-General representing the British Crown|Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Nigeria|Option A|With Nigeria becoming a republic, Dr. Nnamdi Azikiwe transitioned from Governor-General to become the first ceremonial Head of State of the Nigerian Republic.
10.1|How was the Mid-Western Region successfully created prior to the 1963 Republican Constitution?|Through constitutional due process and legislative procedures|By a unilateral military decree issued by the federal parliament|Through a direct mandate from the United Nations trusteeship council|Via a referendum held exclusively by traditional rulers without public vote|Option A|The Mid-Western Region was successfully carved out of the existing Western Region using established constitutional due process mechanisms.
10.1|Which primary institutional link to the British colonial government was officially severed by the 1963 Constitution?|The British monarchy as the source of executive sovereignty|The adoption of the Westminster parliamentary electoral map|The reliance on British pounds sterling for domestic fiscal policy|The use of English as the sole language of legislative debate|Option A|The primary colonial bond severed in 1963 was the British monarchy, transitioning Nigeria from a constitutional monarchy to a fully indigenous republic.
10.1|The creation of the Mid-Western Region added to the federation structure, changing the regional configuration from three regions to how many total regions?|Four distinct administrative regions|Five distinct administrative regions|Six distinct administrative regions|Seven distinct administrative regions|Option A|Prior to 1963, Nigeria had three regions (Northern, Western, Eastern); the creation of the Mid-Western Region increased the total number of regions to four.
10.1|What key characteristic best describes the nature of the presidency held by Dr. Nnamdi Azikiwe under the 1963 Republican Constitution?|Ceremonial and titular headship rather than executive dominance|Absolute executive control over all regional legislatures and armed forces|Dual executive shared equally with the British monarch|Subordinate to the colonial governor-general based in London|Option A|Under the 1963 Constitution, the President served as a ceremonial Head of State, while substantial executive power remained vested in the Prime Minister and cabinet.
10.1|The replacement of the London Privy Council by the Supreme Court of Nigeria signifies which major milestone in Nigerian administrative history?|Complete judicial independence and decolonization of the legal hierarchy|The total abandonment of English common law traditions in local courts|The dissolution of all regional high courts across the federation|The merging of customary courts into international arbitration tribunals|Option A|Localizing the final court of appeal to the Supreme Court of Nigeria marked a crucial step toward complete judicial autonomy and national sovereignty.
10.1|Which major political milestone occurred simultaneously with Nigeria adopting a republican status in October 1963?|Severing legal ties with the British monarchy|Adopting a purely presidential system of government similar to the United States|Granting universal adult suffrage to Northern women for the first time|Merging the Northern and Southern protectorates into a single colony|Option A|The defining feature of the 1963 Republican Constitution was the severance of ties with the British monarchy, establishing Nigeria as a republic on October 1, 1963.
10.1|In the context of the 1963 Republican Constitution, what was the primary significance of establishing the Mid-Western Region?|It expanded the federal structure through constitutional means to accommodate minority groups|It abolished the existing regional structure in favor of a unitary system of government|It served as the first state created exclusively through a military coup d'etat|It reduced federal expenditures by merging two existing administrative zones|Option A|The creation of the Mid-Western Region was a significant constitutional exercise aimed at addressing minority agitations within the old Western Region.

3.1|Who were the Eso Ikoyi in the traditional administrative and military framework of Old Oyo?|A council of seven divine priest-kings|A corps of seventy noble military commanders celebrated for bravery|A network of palace guards serving the Alaafin's household|A tribunal of elder judges in charge of provincial disputes|Option B|The Eso Ikoyi comprised seventy elite noble war commanders who formed the backbone of Oyo military leadership under the Aare Ona Kakanfo.

3.1|Why was the supreme military commander, the Aare Ona Kakanfo, prohibited from residing inside the imperial capital city of Oyo-Ile?|To ensure his troops remained stationed close to international borders|To prevent a military takeover or coup against the central political authority|To maintain his continuous religious ritual purity outside palace grounds|To facilitate direct monitoring of provincial tribute collection|Option B|Stationing the Aare Ona Kakanfo outside the capital prevented military concentration in Oyo-Ile, reducing the risk of military coups against the monarch.
3.1|Which concept best describes the overall administrative system of the Old Oyo Empire?|An absolute monarchy controlled entirely by the divine monarch|A constitutional system based on separation of powers and checks and balances|A decentralized confederation without a centralized military or legal head|A military dictatorship governed directly by army commanders|Option B|The administrative structure of Old Oyo was a balanced constitutional monarchy characterized by reciprocal checks and balances among the Alaafin, Oyo Mesi, Ogboni, and military chiefs.

11.1|What was the primary constitutional purpose of introducing the Federal Character Principle in the 1979 Constitution?|To ensure absolute ideological uniformity across all federating units|To promote national unity and command national loyalty by preventing the dominance of particular ethnic groups|To centralize the recruitment of all civil servants directly under the presidency|To eliminate state governments and establish a unitary state structure|Option B|The Federal Character Principle was designed to reflect national diversity in public institutions, thereby fostering unity, stability, and a sense of belonging among all groups.

11.1|Which organ of government exercised legislative power at the federal level under the 1979 Constitution?|The National Assembly|The Federal Executive Council|The Supreme Military Council|The Council of State|Option A|Legislative authority under the 1979 Presidential Constitution was vested in a bicameral National Assembly comprising the Senate and the House of Representatives.
11.1|How did the executive branch differ fundamentally under the 1979 Constitution compared to the preceding parliamentary arrangement?|Cabinet members had to be sitting members of the National Assembly|The President was exclusively accountable to the judiciary for policy decisions|Ministers were appointed by the President and were not simultaneously members of the legislature|Executive actions required prior unanimous approval from all state governors|Option C|Under the presidential system, there is a strict separation of personnel where executive ministers cannot simultaneously serve as members of the legislature.

11.1|What institutional mechanism under the 1979 Constitution served as a check on the executive branch's power to make high-level appointments?|Confirmation powers vested in the Senate|Approval required from traditional rulers|Veto power exercised by state assemblies|Direct referendum by the general electorate|Option A|The National Assembly, specifically the Senate, served as a crucial check on presidential power by requiring confirmation for ministerial nominees and other key public appointments.

4.1|How does the Umuada institution contribute uniquely to traditional Igbo administrative and conflict resolution processes?|By acting as an elite assembly of daughters of the lineage who mediate disputes and influence family decisions|By commanding the village defense forces during external invasions|By serving as the exclusive economic tax collectors for market stalls|By performing secret initiation rites exclusively for male titleholders|Option A|The Umuada is the influential assembly of daughters of a lineage who leverage their unique status to mediate family conflicts, exert moral authority, and influence community decisions.
4.1|In a political system characterized by Igbo Enwe Eze, how are major policy decisions typically finalized?|Through decree issued by a hereditary paramount ruler|Through direct consensus-building among adult male citizens and elders|Through majority voting enforced by a standing police force|Through oracle consultation dictating absolute commands without debate|Option B|Decision-making in traditional acephalous Igbo societies relies heavily on open discussions and direct consensus-building among community members rather than royal decrees or majority voting.
4.1|Which concept best contrasts with the traditional administrative system found in Igbo land?|Acephalous democracy|Segmentary governance|Centralized monarchy|Consensual assembly|Option C|Traditional Igbo administration is famously acephalous and decentralized, which stands in direct contrast to centralized monarchical systems found in other parts of Nigeria.

1.1|Which of the following best defines a cephalous or centralized pre-colonial administrative system in Nigeria?|A system characterized by centralized authority, hierarchical governance structures, and formal political offices|A decentralized community ruled entirely by age grades and secret societies without a king|A nomadic tribal alliance operating without permanent territorial boundaries|A democratic confederation of autonomous village assemblies with equal voting power|Option A|Cephalous societies feature institutionalized centralized leadership, distinct hierarchies, and defined political offices such as kingdoms and empires.
1.1|How are acephalous or non-centralized pre-colonial Nigerian societies primarily structurally organized?|Into hereditary feudal estates tied to a central monarchical treasury|Into segmentary lineages and decentralized village groups sharing power horizontally|Under a strict Islamic caliphate system headed by an Emir|Under a military dictatorship controlled by a standing professional army|Option B|Acephalous societies, such as the Igbo and Tiv, lack a single centralized head, organizing instead through kinship, segmentary lineages, and decentralized councils.

10.1|Which judicial institution replaced the London Privy Council as the highest and final court of appeal for Nigeria in 1963?|The Supreme Court of Nigeria|The Federal Court of Appeal|The West African Court of Appeal|The International Court of Justice|Option A|The 1963 Republican Constitution abolished appeals to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in London, making the Supreme Court of Nigeria the ultimate appellate tribunal.
10.1|What significant structural change occurred regarding Nigeria's internal federation map during the era of the 1963 Constitution?|The Mid-Western Region was created via constitutional due process|Lagos was excised entirely to become an independent international protectorate|The Northern Region was split into three distinct self-governing provinces|Eastern Nigeria was dissolved and merged temporarily with the Western Region|Option A|The Mid-Western Region was successfully carved out of the Western Region through formal constitutional procedures under the First Republic.
10.1|What was the primary constitutional status of the Nigerian Head of State under the 1963 Republican Constitution?|Ceremonial with limited executive powers exercised on ministerial advice|Executive president with direct command over military and legislative vetoes|Prime ministerial head who concurrently held the title of Commander-in-Chief|Absolute monarch holding traditional sovereign authority over all regions|Option A|Under the 1963 Constitution, the President served as a ceremonial Head of State while executive power rested with the Prime Minister and cabinet.
10.1|By replacing the British monarch with an indigenous president, what core administrative principle was achieved in 1963?|Complete autochthony and domestic ownership of the highest symbol of state authority|The immediate unification of all regional civil services into a single federal bureaucracy|The permanent abolition of the bicameral federal parliamentary legislative structure|The complete centralization of police and revenue-generation powers in Lagos|Option A|Severing ties with the British Crown established national autochthony, meaning the constitution derived its ultimate legal authority from within Nigeria.
10.1|Which legal mechanism was strictly utilized to create the Mid-Western Region in 1963?|Constitutional due process outlined in the independence legal framework|A military decree issued unilaterally by the federal executive council|A popular referendum mandated by the United Nations Trusteeship Council|An executive order signed exclusively by the Prime Minister without regional consent|Option A|The creation of the Mid-Western Region followed the rigorous constitutional due process provisions stipulated in the 1960 independence constitution.
10.1|The transition from a dominion status to a republic in 1963 primarily altered Nigeria's relationship with which entity?|The British Crown and its constitutional oversight mechanisms|The United Nations Security Council permanent membership structure|The Commonwealth of Nations economic and trade tariff agreements|The Organization of African Unity charter obligations and protocols|Option A|Becoming a republic meant Nigeria no longer recognized the British monarch as its sovereign head, altering its constitutional relationship with the British Crown.
10.1|Why was the replacement of the London Privy Council with the Supreme Court of Nigeria considered a milestone in judicial administration?|It localized judicial finality and reinforced national sovereignty|It introduced Sharia law as the exclusive supreme law across all southern regions|It gave regional governors the power to overturn supreme court rulings|It subordinated all customary courts directly to colonial administrative officers|Option A|The shift localized the highest court of appeal, ensuring that final legal interpretations rested entirely within Nigerian judicial institutions rather than a foreign council.
10.1|What administrative designation did Nigeria officially adopt upon the implementation of the 1963 Constitution?|Federal Republic|Confederal Commonwealth|Unitary Kingdom|Democratic Protectorate|Option A|The 1963 Constitution formally established Nigeria as a Federal Republic, marking its departure from a constitutional monarchy within the Commonwealth realms.
11.1|What fundamental governance model replaced the Westminster parliamentary system in Nigeria under the 1979 Constitution?|The French Semi-Presidential model|The American Executive Presidential system|The Swiss Direct Democracy model|The Soviet Socialist Council model|Option B|The 1979 Constitution marked a total departure from the British Westminster parliamentary system by adopting the American-style Executive Presidential system.
11.1|Under the 1979 Presidential Constitution, how are the roles of Head of State and Head of Government designated?|Both roles are vested in a single elected Executive President|The Head of State is ceremonial while a Prime Minister is Head of Government|The Head of State is chosen by the judiciary while the Prime Minister runs the cabinet|The roles are rotated annually among regional governors|Option A|Unlike the Westminster system where these roles are separated between a ceremonial president and a prime minister, the Executive President holds both positions simultaneously.
