11.1|How did the 1979 Constitution attempt to curb ethnic-based regional politics through political party regulations?|By mandating that political parties demonstrate a strict national spread in their membership and leadership|By requiring all parties to be funded entirely by international donors|By banning political parties that did not originate in the northern region|By allowing only independent candidates to contest presidential elections|Option A|To prevent the recurrence of ethnically fragmented First Republic parties, the 1979 Constitution required political parties to exhibit a broad national spread across the federation.
11.1|Which branch of government under the 1979 Constitution holds the primary responsibility for lawmaking at the national level?|The National Assembly|The Federal Executive Council|The Supreme Judicial Council|The Council of State|Option A|The National Assembly serves as the bicameral legislature tasked with enacting laws for the federation under the presidential system.
11.1|In the context of the 1979 Executive Presidential system, what role does the President play regarding the armed forces?|Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces|Chief Justice of the Federation|President of the Senate|Chairman of the National Electoral Commission|Option A|As both Head of State and Head of Government, the Executive President exercises supreme constitutional command over the nation armed forces.
11.1|What distinguishes the tenure and survival of the executive branch under a presidential system like Nigeria 1979 from the Westminster model?|The executive depends on a majority vote of confidence in parliament|The executive serves a fixed term and is not politically dependent on a legislative vote of confidence|The executive can dissolve parliament at will without legal checks|The executive tenure is determined by traditional monarchs|Option B|Under the presidential system, the executive enjoys a fixed constitutional tenure and does not fall due to a legislative vote of no confidence.
11.1|Which structural feature of the National Assembly was established by the 1979 Constitution to reflect federalism?|A unicameral parliament consisting only of population-based representatives|A bicameral legislature comprising the Senate and the House of Representatives|A tripartite parliament with regional veto powers|A council of elders functioning as the upper chamber|Option B|The 1979 Constitution created a bicameral National Assembly featuring a Senate for equal state representation and a House of Representatives based on population.
11.1|Why is the shift to the 1979 Presidential Constitution considered a major watershed in Nigerian administrative history?|It completely eliminated bureaucratic structures inherited from the colonial era|It decentralized all national security powers to local government councils|It dismantled the British parliamentary tradition and introduced a presidential model with checks and balances|It replaced the federal system with a unitary government structure|Option C|The transition represented a fundamental institutional engineering effort to address the structural flaws of the First Republic through presidentialism and constitutional checks and balances.

1.1|In pre-colonial Nigerian societies, what role did customary taboos and ancestral lineage play in governance?|They served as ideological instruments for social control and moral compliance|They were purely economic measures used for agricultural tax collection|They were foreign laws introduced by early European explorers|They were temporary rules abandoned during times of war|Option A|Customary taboos and ancestral reverence acted as powerful normative frameworks that regulated behavior and reinforced political and social authority without formal police forces.
1.1|Which of the following best differentiates a centralized pre-colonial state from a non-centralized one in Nigeria?|Centralized states featured distinct political hierarchies and institutionalized leadership, whereas non-centralized states used segmentary lineage organization|Centralized states relied exclusively on written laws, while non-centralized states used oral history|Centralized states prohibited all religious practices, while non-centralized states were theocratic|Centralized states had no taxation mechanisms, while non-centralized states taxed heavily|Option A|The core distinction lies in the institutional structure; centralized states had formal hierarchical offices and rulers, whereas non-centralized societies distributed authority horizontally across kinship lines.
1.1|What structural feature was most prominent in the Tiv society during the pre-colonial era?|A centralized emirate council headed by a single sultan|A segmentary lineage system lacking a centralized government|A feudal system with landed aristocracy and serfdom|A constitutional monarchy with a parliament|Option B|The Tiv are a classic example of an acephalous, segmentary lineage society in pre-colonial Nigeria that organized political and social life without a central state authority.
1.1|The exercise of power in many pre-colonial Nigerian centralized systems was heavily intertwined with which of the following concepts?|Secular republicanism|Sacred monarchy and divine sanction|Capitalist market forces|Bureaucratic neutrality|Option B|Rulers in centralized polities often derived their legitimacy from religious sanction and sacred monarchy, where the king was viewed as a divine representative or intermediary with higher powers.
1.1|Why are segmentary societies often referred to as acephalous?|Because they had multiple kings ruling simultaneously|Because they lacked a single head or centralized seat of government|Because they were governed entirely by military generals|Because their leaders were chosen exclusively from foreign lands|Option B|The term acephalous literally translates to headless, signifying the absence of a single central head of state or centralized political hierarchy.
1.1|Which factor served as a primary cohesive force in maintaining solidarity within non-centralized pre-colonial Nigerian communities?|A centralized police force maintained by taxes|Kinship ties, shared ancestry, and customary traditions|Direct administrative orders from a paramount chief|Mandatory military conscription laws|Option B|In the absence of a central coercive state apparatus, non-centralized communities relied on kinship, shared ancestry, customs, and social institutions to maintain order and cohesion.

13.1|From an administrative perspective, why is the 1976 Local Government Reform regarded as a watershed moment in Nigerian public administration?|It established local government as an autonomous tier with constitutional and financial recognition|It completely decentralized military command structures to municipal councilors|It transferred national revenue collection responsibilities to local tax offices|It converted local government areas into military garrison districts|Option A|The 1976 reform fundamentally transformed local governance by institutionalizing local government as a recognized third tier with statutory financial provisions.

13.1|How did the 1976 Local Government Reform manage the administrative and political role of traditional rulers?|By appointing paramount chiefs as executive chairmen of local councils|By completely dissolving traditional institutions across all regions|By insulating traditional rulers and restricting them to advisory councils|By granting traditional rulers absolute veto power over local bylaws|Option C|To modernize administration and minimize political friction, traditional rulers were insulated from partisan politics and confined to advisory roles.
13.1|Which significant administrative innovation regarding political leadership was introduced by the 1984 Dasuki Committee and subsequent 1988 reforms?|Introduction of Executive Chairmen for local government councils|Establishment of lifetime unelected sole administrators for councils|Delegation of local executive powers strictly to state governors|Creation of a collegiate presidential cabinet system for districts|Option A|The Dasuki Committee recommendations and Babangida reforms promoted grassroots democracy and clear executive accountability by introducing Executive Chairmen.
13.1|What major shift in financial administration accompanied the 1988 reforms following the Dasuki Committee framework?|Centralization of all council funds in state treasury fixed accounts|Introduction of direct revenue transfers to local government treasuries|Prohibition of any federal intervention in local budgeting processes|Abolition of federal revenue allocations in favor of local self-taxation|Option B|The reforms ensured financial autonomy and timeliness by implementing direct revenue transfers to local government treasuries.
13.1|The inclusion of local governments as the third tier of government in 1976 primarily aimed to achieve which objective?|To decentralize government powers and bring development closer to the grassroots|To merge local authorities with state ministries of local government|To eliminate the need for any federal taxation policy in rural areas|To transition the country into a unitary governance model|Option A|The primary philosophy of the 1976 reform was effective decentralization to accelerate grassroots development and democratic participation.
13.1|What was a primary consequence of insulating traditional rulers into advisory councils during the 1976 reforms?|Their complete financial ruin and forfeiture of all properties|Separation of traditional dignity and cultural authority from partisan local politics|The complete eradication of chieftaincy titles across the federation|Their appointment as permanent civil service heads of local departments|Option B|Insulation protected traditional institutions from political manipulation while preserving their cultural prestige through advisory councils.
13.1|Which governing body or committee report heavily influenced the structural and executive modifications of local administration in 1984?|The Udoji Public Service Review Commission|The Dasuki Committee on Local Government Reforms|The Dasuki Panel on Federal Civil Service Reorganization|The Williams Judicial Commission of Inquiry|Option B|The Dasuki Committee of 1984 critically reviewed local government administration and paved the way for subsequent restructuring under Babangida in 1988.
13.1|Which combination of structural reforms defines the evolution of Nigerian local government from 1976 to 1988?|Uniform single tier creation followed by Executive Chairmen and direct revenue transfers|Multi-tier fragmentation followed by abolition of local councils altogether|Regional administrative autonomy followed by military caretaker management exclusively|Centralized unitary boards followed by traditional monarchy restoration|Option A|The timeline progressed from the uniform single-tier structure and 3rd tier status in 1976 to executive chairmen and direct revenue transfers under Dasuki and Babangida.
12.1|What was a major structural innovation introduced into the Nigerian civil service by the 1974 Udoji Commission?|Unified Grading and Salary Structure (UGSS)|Abolition of the cabinet system|Restoration of career Permanent Secretaries|Decentralization of all regional budgets|Option A|The Udoji Commission of 1974 introduced the Unified Grading and Salary Structure to eliminate pay disparities across the public sector.
12.1|Which modern management techniques were first introduced into the Nigerian public administration framework by the Udoji Commission of 1974?|Management by Objectives (MBO) and Planning Programming Budgeting System (PPBS)|Zero-Based Budgeting and Total Quality Management|Just-In-Time production and Six Sigma|SWOT analysis and balanced scorecards|Option A|The Udoji Commission introduced modern result-oriented management concepts like MBO and PPBS to modernize public service operations.
12.1|Under the 1988 Babangida civil service reform based on the Phillips Report, who was designated as both the Chief Executive and the Accounting Officer of a ministry?|The Minister|The Permanent Secretary|The Director-General|The Head of Service|Option A|The 1988 reform shifted administrative power by making the political Minister both the Chief Executive and the Accounting Officer.
12.1|What change did the 1988 Babangida reform introduce regarding the traditional position of the Permanent Secretary?|Replaced it with a political Director-General tenure|Abolished the office entirely without replacement|Made it a lifetime elected legislative seat|Subordinated it directly to local government chairmen|Option A|The 1988 reform re-designated the Permanent Secretary position as a Director-General whose tenure became linked to the political administration.
12.1|What core principle defined the single-ministry professionalization policy mandated under the 1988 Babangida reform?|Officers spent their entire career within one ministry to master its specialized functions|Officers rotated across all government ministries every six months|Civil servants were mandated to work part-time in the private sector|Recruitment was restricted strictly to foreign consultants|Option A|Single-ministry professionalization required officers to build specialized career paths within a single ministry rather than moving across the broader civil service.
12.1|Which administrative review panel of 1997 was responsible for reversing key structural changes of the 1988 Babangida reform?|Ayida Panel|Gorsuch Commission|Udoji Commission|Phillips Panel|Option A|The Ayida Panel of 1997 reviewed the 1988 reforms and recommended reversing several provisions to restore traditional civil service neutrality.
12.1|What key traditional civil service status was restored by the Ayida Panel of 1997?|Permanent career status of the Permanent Secretary|Unified salary grading across state corporations|Ministerial status as sole accounting officer|Political tenure for Directors-General|Option A|The Ayida Panel restored the permanent and non-political career status of the Permanent Secretary, undoing the 1988 political tenure arrangement.
12.1|The Phillips Report served as the primary blueprint and intellectual foundation for which major administrative reform in Nigeria?|1988 Babangida Reform|1974 Udoji Commission|1954 Gorsuch Commission|1997 Ayida Panel|Option A|The 1988 Babangida reform was heavily guided and shaped by the recommendations contained in the Phillips Report.
12.1|How did the 1988 Babangida reform alter the traditional relationship between political office holders and career civil servants?|It politicized the top administrative tier by making the top bureaucratic head a political appointee|It completely removed ministers from any administrative oversight|It granted career bureaucrats the power to veto legislative bills|It merged the civil service commission with the judiciary|Option A|The 1988 reform altered administrative dynamics by tying the top bureaucratic role to political tenure, reducing traditional bureaucratic insulation.

2.1|Which major economic transition characterized the evolution of Niger Delta city-states such as Bonny and Nembe during the nineteenth century?|From agricultural subsistence to industrial manufacturing|From the transatlantic slave trade to legitimate commerce in palm oil|From pastoral nomadism to sedentary maritime fishing|From mercantilism to heavy metallic mining|Option B|The Niger Delta city-states shifted their economic base from the slave trade to palm oil legitimate commerce as European demand changed.
2.1|What was the foundational socio-economic and political unit of the Niger Delta city-states that replaced traditional kinship groups for trade mobilization?|The Age-Grade Guild|The Communal Land Trust|The Canoe House System|The Royal Chartered Monopoly|Option C|The Canoe House System (Wari) functioned as a corporate trading entity and military unit designed to mobilize resources for the palm oil trade.
2.1|Who held supreme political and mercantile authority over a typical Niger Delta Canoe House entity?|The Chief Priest of the Oracle|The Amanyanabo or merchant chief|The Head of the Secret Intelligence Guild|The Master General of the Armies|Option B|Merchant chiefs and rulers known as the Amanyanabo presided over the political and commercial structures of the city-states and Canoe Houses.
2.1|What role did secret societies like the Ekpe play within the administration of Southern Nigerian coastal societies?|They served exclusively as religious burial fraternities|They enforced contracts, maintained public order, and regulated trade law|They functioned as standing mercenary armies against inland kingdoms|They regulated agricultural crop rotation and land tenure exclusively|Option B|Secret societies like Ekpe acted as powerful judicial and executive bodies that enforced contracts, resolved disputes, and ensured public order.
2.1|Which of the following coastal societies of Southern Nigeria is specifically grouped alongside Bonny, Nembe, and Kalabari in the historical evolution of the region?|The Oyo Empire|The Itsekiri kingdom|The Sokoto Caliphate|The Kanem-Bornu Empire|Option B|The Itsekiri, along with Bonny, Nembe, and Kalabari, formed part of the prominent coastal societies and kingdoms of Southern Nigeria.
2.1|How did the structural nature of the Canoe House System differ from traditional kinship-based family units?|It was strictly religious and excluded commercial activities|It operated as a corporate enterprise capable of owning large fleets of trade canoes and slaves|It was entirely democratic with annual rotation of leadership among all adults|It operated solely under direct colonial government supervision|Option B|The Canoe House was structured like a corporate business capable of holding property, managing large labor forces, and pooling capital for trade.
2.1|In the context of nineteenth-century Niger Delta history, what did the term legitimate commerce primarily denote?|Trade conducted exclusively through barter without currency|The legal trade in non-slaves commodities such as palm oil and kernels|Official trade sanctioned directly by the British Crown parliament|Legalized domestic slave trading under new administrative oversight|Option B|Legitimate commerce referred to the substitution of the slave trade with trade in natural produce, predominantly palm oil.
2.1|Which administrative function was vital for merchant chiefs operating within the competitive palm oil networks of the coastal city-states?|Managing trans-Saharan caravan routes|Controlling access to European supercargoes and inland trade monopoly routes|Regulating gold mining standards in the hinterlands|Supervising railway construction across swamp forests|Option B|Merchant chiefs maintained control by mediating between European traders on the coast and inland producers, dominating trade routes.
2.1|What primary mechanism did the Ekpe secret society utilize to ensure compliance with commercial debts and civic regulations?|Imposing spiritual sanctions, public boycotts, and strict judicial enforcement|Levying direct income taxes on foreign European visitors|Executing military coups against traditional monarchs|Organizing general strikes of canoe paddlers|Option A|Ekpe used ritual sanctions, ostracism, and judicial enforcement to compel compliance with commercial contracts and community laws.
2.1|Why was the transition from the slave trade to palm oil trade a critical turning point for the administrative structures of Southern Nigerian city-states?|It required a more labor-intensive, corporate organization like the Canoe House to manage bulk production and transport|It led to the complete collapse of all indigenous political institutions|It forced coastal city-states to abandon maritime trade entirely for farming|It required centralized bureaucratic control modeled after European parliaments|Option A|The palm oil trade demanded large-scale labor organization for harvesting, processing, and transporting oil, which the Canoe House system uniquely provided.
1.1|Which fundamental political distinction characterizes pre-colonial Nigerian societies in the study of administrative history?|Feudal states versus industrial capitalist republics|Centralized cephalous kingdoms versus non-centralized acephalous societies|Colonial protectorates versus sovereign city-states|Monarchical autocracies versus modern democratic confederations|Option B|Pre-colonial Nigerian administrative structures are primarily classified into centralized cephalous systems like kingdoms and empires, and non-centralized acephalous systems like segmentary societies.|
1.1|What term best describes societies in pre-colonial Nigeria that lacked a centralized political authority or single institutionalized ruling class?|Cephalous kingdoms|Acephalous or segmentary societies|Theocratic caliphates|Feudal monarchies|Option B|Acephalous or segmentary societies, such as the pre-colonial Igbo and Tiv, operated without a single centralized political authority or permanent institutionalized leadership.|
1.1|Which of the following societies is a classic historical example of a non-centralized acephalous structure in pre-colonial Nigeria?|The Sokoto Caliphate|The Old Oyo Empire|The Igbo and Tiv societies|The Kanem-Borno Empire|Option C|The Igbo and Tiv are prime examples of acephalous societies that relied on decentralized, lineage-based, and segmentary socio-political arrangements rather than centralized kingship.|
1.1|How was political authority primarily legitimized in centralized pre-colonial Nigerian kingdoms and empires?|Through universal adult suffrage and periodic elections|Through sacred monarchy, royal lineage, and religious rituals|Through written constitutional law and parliamentary statutes|Through international treaties and trade agreements|Option B|Centralized systems relied heavily on sacred monarchy, ancestral lineage, customary taboos, and religious rituals to establish and maintain political legitimacy.|
1.1|What administrative feature distinguished cephalous political systems in pre-colonial Nigeria from acephalous systems?|The complete absence of any social norms or rules|The presence of a structured hierarchy, recognized ruling authority, and centralized institutions|The practice of nomadic pastoralism exclusively|The total rejection of any form of religious practice|Option B|Cephalous systems featured structured political hierarchies, institutionalized offices, and recognized central ruling authorities like kings, emirs, or obas.|
1.1|Which mechanism served as a powerful social and political constraint against the abuse of power in many traditional pre-colonial Nigerian societies?|Customary taboos and sacred religious rituals|Military intervention by foreign mercenaries|Strictly codified written penal codes enforced by police|Standing professional labor unions|Option A|Customary taboos and religious rituals acted as vital checks on leadership, ensuring that rulers respected ancestral laws and societal norms out of fear of supernatural retribution.|
1.1|In segmentary acephalous societies of pre-colonial Nigeria, how was social order and administration largely maintained?|Through a standing royal army commanded by a paramount monarch|Through kinship ties, ancestral lineage, and decentralized council decisions|Through bureaucratic ministries appointed by a central governor|Through taxation administered by a unified federal treasury|Option B|Acephalous societies maintained order organically through kinship networks, elders' councils, age grades, and ancestral lineage systems rather than centralized bureaucratic apparatuses.|
1.1|What conceptual role did religion and cosmology play in the administrative systems of pre-colonial centralized Nigerian states?|They were strictly separated from governance through secular legislation|They provided the foundational basis of authority and sacred legitimacy for rulers|They served solely as economic enterprises for revenue generation|They were introduced exclusively by European colonial administrators|Option B|Religion was deeply intertwined with governance, providing the spiritual framework, divine right, and sacred legitimacy that anchored the ruler's authority.|
1.1|Which structural element was most characteristic of governance in the Sokoto Caliphate and Old Oyo Empire?|Segmentary village democracy without chiefs|Centralized administrative machinery headed by a supreme ruler|A complete lack of territorial division or taxation|Nomadic councils with rotating leadership every year|Option B|Both the Sokoto Caliphate and the Old Oyo Empire were centralized states featuring complex administrative machinery, hierarchical offices, and supreme rulers like the Caliph or the Alaafin.|
1.1|Why is the study of pre-colonial social organization essential for understanding the history of Nigerian public administration?|It demonstrates that pre-colonial societies lacked any form of order or governance|It reveals the indigenous administrative foundations, authority bases, and governance models upon which later systems were built|It proves that colonial rule was entirely unnecessary for social evolution|It focuses exclusively on modern constitutional law and civil service reforms|Option B|Studying pre-colonial structures uncovers the rich indigenous foundations of authority, social control, and governance that pre-dated and often influenced subsequent administrative arrangements.
3.1|Who served as the supreme monarch and head of the central government in the traditional administrative structure of the Oyo Empire?|The Bashorun|The Alaafin|The Aare Ona Kakanfo|The Ogboni|Option B|The Alaafin of Oyo was the supreme monarch and central head of government in the historical administration of the Oyo Empire.
3.1|What role did the Oyo Mesi play within the governance framework of the Oyo Empire?|They served as resident provincial monitors|They commanded the regular military forces in border wars|They acted as the council of seven kingmaker chiefs led by the Bashorun|They functioned exclusively as an independent judicial court for treason|Option C|The Oyo Mesi consisted of seven prominent kingmaker chiefs led by the Bashorun who held the authority to select and check the Alaafin.
3.1|Which traditional mechanism was utilized by the Oyo Mesi to check the tyrannical rule of an unpopular Alaafin?|Imprisonment in the imperial dungeon|Public trial and execution by the Ogboni society|Sending an empty calabash or parrot eggs to compel ritual suicide|Banishment to a foreign territory across the river Niger|Option C|When an Alaafin became tyrannical, the Oyo Mesi would present an empty calabash or parrot eggs, which symbolically compelled the monarch to commit ritual suicide.
3.1|What was the primary political function of the Ogboni society in the ancient Oyo Empire?|To collect annual taxes from all provincial towns|To mediate political disputes and check the excesses of both the Alaafin and the Oyo Mesi|To lead military expeditions into rival territories|To serve as the supreme body of kingmakers for the imperial throne|Option B|The Ogboni society played a crucial mediating role, balancing power and helping to resolve conflicts between the Alaafin and the Oyo Mesi.
3.1|Who were the Ajele in the context of the Oyo Empire provincial administration?|Elite commanders of the cavalry units|Resident monitors or agents sent to oversee provincial towns and collect tribute|Spiritual priests responsible for royal coronation rituals|Foreign diplomats representing neighboring kingdoms|Option A|The Ajele were administrative representatives and resident monitors dispatched by the central government to oversee provincial territories and ensure loyalty.
3.1|How many elite military commanders made up the group known as the Eso Ikoyi in the Oyo military hierarchy?|Twelve|Fifty|Seventy|One hundred|Option C|The Eso Ikoyi comprised seventy elite military commanders who formed the backbone of the Oyo imperial defense and cavalry.
3.1|What was the supreme military commander of the Oyo Empire's armed forces called?|The Bashorun|The Aare Ona Kakanfo|The Ajele|The Onikoyi|Option B|The Aare Ona Kakanfo held the title of supreme military commander, tasked with leading the army into major campaigns.
3.1|What strict traditional convention governed the operational tenure of the Aare Ona Kakanfo during wartime?|He was required to return home after precisely forty days|He had to secure total victory or face ritual death on the battlefield|He was forbidden from commanding more than half of the cavalry|He shared equal administrative power with the Alaafin during crises|Option B|The Aare Ona Kakanfo was bound by tradition to achieve total victory in battle or else commit suicide if defeated.
3.1|Which administrative official held the position of leader of the Oyo Mesi kingmaker council?|The Aare Ona Kakanfo|The Bashorun|The Onikoyi|The Ooni|Option B|The Bashorun served as the head of the Oyo Mesi and played a leading role in both kingmaking and checking royal authority.
3.1|Which of the following best describes the structural nature of the Oyo Empire central administration?|An absolute dictatorship with zero institutional restraints|A centralized constitutional monarchy featuring well-defined checks and balances|A decentralized confederation of independent city-states|A purely military junta ruled by frontline field generals|Option B|The Oyo Empire utilized a sophisticated constitutional monarchy system incorporating institutional checks and balances such as the Oyo Mesi and the Ogboni society.
4.1|Which fundamental political concept is encapsulated by the traditional Igbo maxim Igbo Enwe Eze?|Centralized monarchical absolutism|Segmentary and non-hierarchical democracy|Feudalistic land tenure system|Colonial indirect rule assimilation|Option B|The phrase Igbo Enwe Eze translates to the Igbo have no king highlighting their traditional stateless or acephalous democratic structure.|
4.1|What is the primary function of the Umunna in traditional Igbo administration?|Serving as the supreme royal judiciary|Acting as the extended family lineage council led by the eldest male|Enforcing market taxes on behalf of paramount chiefs|Commanding the external military defense league|Option B|The Umunna represents the foundational kinship and lineage unit rooted in extended family ties and headed by the Okpara.|
4.1|What role does the sacred Ofo staff play within the traditional administration of the Umunna?|It acts as a monetary currency for trade|It serves as a symbol of spiritual authority truth and justice held by the Okpara|It functions as a weapon of war for the age grades|It is used exclusively by the Umuada to settle marital disputes|Option B|The Ofo is a revered ritual symbol of authority truth and moral integrity wielded by the lineage head during deliberations.|
4.1|Who constitutes the membership of the Oha-na-Eze in a traditional Igbo community?|Only the wealthy title holders of the Ozo society|Exclusive membership of the female Umuada assembly|All adult males gathered in a broad village assembly|Delegates appointed by external colonial administrators|Option C|The Oha-na-Eze is the supreme general assembly comprising all adult males of the community where direct consensus democracy is practiced.|
4.1|Which group represents the council of elders responsible for advisory governance in traditional Igbo settings?|Umuada|Ndichie|Uke|Ozo|Option B|The Ndichie are respected elders who provide wise counsel and historical precedent to complement community decision-making.|
4.1|What is the primary socio-political significance of the Ozo or Nze institution in Igbo land?|It regulates agricultural seasons and rainfall rituals|It provides a title society recognizing personal integrity wealth and leadership prestige|It serves exclusively as a military fighting force against invaders|It manages internal household chores and market sanitation|Option B|The Ozo or Nze title society is an elite brotherhood symbolizing high moral integrity community service and leadership status.|
4.1|What are the primary duties assigned to Age Grades such as Uke or Ogbo within the traditional administration?|Public works community mobilization and law enforcement|Adjudication of intricate land ownership disputes|Spiritual divination and ancestral worship ceremonies|Enactment of supreme laws binding all neighboring clans|Option A|Age grades are vibrant youth organizations mobilized for communal labor infrastructure maintenance and public security enforcement.|
4.1|What unique structural role do the Umuada perform in traditional Igbo socio-political systems?|They act as the standing army during inter-village wars|They serve as daughters of the lineage acting as powerful mediators and peacebuilders|They hold absolute veto power over all male assembly decisions|They collect agricultural tributes from non-indigenous settlers|Option B|The Umuada comprises daughters of the lineage who wield significant moral authority and act as effective arbiters in family and community conflicts.|
4.1|Which decision-making process was predominantly utilized in the traditional acephalous democracy of the Igbo?|Majority voting with a strict legislative quorum|Autocratic decree by the oldest living patriarch|Direct consensus building through extensive deliberation|Appointment of representatives via a secret ballot system|Option C|Traditional Igbo governance favored participatory democracy centered on reaching a general consensus through open dialogue among members.|
4.1|Why is the traditional Igbo political system frequently classified by political scientists as acephalous?|Because it was entirely devoid of any legal framework or rules|Because it operated without a centralized monarch or singular supreme ruler|Because political power was concentrated exclusively in the hands of women|Because administrative decisions were dictated by foreign oracles|Option B|Acephalous literally means headless describing societies like the Igbo that function efficiently without a centralized hierarchical monarchy or king.|
5.1|Which historical event led to the establishment of a centralized Islamic theocracy under the Sultan of Sokoto?|The 1804 Sokoto Jihad led by Usman Dan Fodio|The 1914 Amalgamation of Northern and Southern Nigeria|The 1903 British conquest of the Sokoto Caliphate|The 1897 British overthrow of the Benin Kingdom|Option A|The 1804 Sokoto Jihad spearheaded by Usman Dan Fodio successfully established a centralized Islamic theocracy across the region under the supreme leadership of the Sultan of Sokoto.
5.1|What title was held by the supreme spiritual and political leader of the centralized Islamic theocracy established after the 1804 Sokoto Jihad?|Sarkin Musulmi|Waziri|Madawaki|Hakimi|Option A|The Sarkin Musulmi, or Sultan of Sokoto, served as the central spiritual and political head of the entire Sokoto Caliphate system.

1.1|What primarily held non-centralized societies together politically and socially in the absence of a central king?|Kinship ties, ancestral lineages, and segmentary community associations|A standing royal army and a centralized police force|A unified tax collection bureau and standing treasury|State-mandated religious laws enforced by royal executioners|Option A|Without a king, non-centralized societies relied on kinship bonds, extended families, lineage systems, and consensus-based community councils to maintain order.
1.1|Which term accurately denotes a political system where authority is diffused among multiple segments rather than concentrated in a single supreme ruler?|Segmentary system|Unitary federation|Absolute autocracy|Oligarchic empire|Option A|A segmentary system describes acephalous communities where authority is distributed across equal and balancing kinship segments or lineage groups.
1.1|Why is the study of pre-colonial administrative systems essential for understanding modern Nigerian public administration?|It provides the historical foundation and indigenous roots from which contemporary administrative practices evolved|It proves that modern governance structures were entirely imported without local adaptation|It demonstrates that pre-colonial societies had no formal rules or governance mechanisms|It establishes that centralized states are the only viable form of administration in Africa|Option A|Examining pre-colonial systems reveals the indigenous values, traditions, and structural foundations that continue to influence modern Nigerian administrative culture.

3.1|How many elite military commanders made up the renowned Eso Ikoyi warrior guild in the Oyo military hierarchy?|Fifty commanders|Seventy commanders|Ninety commanders|One hundred commanders|Option B|The Eso Ikoyi comprised seventy elite military commanders who formed the backbone of the Oyo imperial army.

3.1|What was the primary political consequence if an Alaafin ignored the constitutional rejection symbolized by the empty calabash?|He was exiled to a foreign land|He was demoted to a provincial governor|He was compelled to commit ritual suicide|He was stripped of his royal wives|Option C|When the Oyo Mesi rejected an Alaafin, tradition strictly mandated that he commit ritual suicide to maintain political equilibrium and spiritual order.

2.1|Which traditional political and social institution served as the foundational corporate and military unit in states like Bonny and Kalabari?|The Age-Grade Guild|The Paramount Monarchy Council|The Canoe House System|The Priesthood Oracle Syndicate|Option C|The Canoe House System (Wari) functioned as a corporate socio-commercial and military unit that organized trade operations, defense, and governance in the Delta city-states.
2.1|What title was typically held by the powerful merchant chiefs who headed the individual Canoe Houses in the Niger Delta?|Amanyanabo|Oba|Olu|Eze|Option A|The Amanyanabo or leading merchant heads managed the Canoe Houses, though the term Amanyanabo often designated the royal town ruler, while house heads managed corporate trading entities.
2.1|How did secret societies such as the Ekpe primarily contribute to the administrative stability of Southern Nigerian coastal societies?|By conducting spiritual divination for rainfall and harvests|By enforcing commercial contracts and maintaining public order|By organizing military conscription for territorial expansion|By collecting centralized taxes for foreign diplomats|Option B|Secret societies like Ekpe acted as powerful juridical and executive institutions that enforced contracts, regulated commerce, and maintained internal public order among traders.
2.1|Which specific Southern Nigerian society is historically grouped alongside Bonny, Nembe, and Kalabari as a prominent coastal kingdom of the Niger Delta?|Itsekiri|Nupe|Kanuri|Tiv|Option A|The Itsekiri kingdom, located in the western Niger Delta, shares historical and administrative characteristics with eastern Delta city-states like Bonny, Nembe, and Kalabari.
2.1|What was a major structural consequence of replacing the slave trade with palm oil commerce in the Niger Delta?|The complete collapse of maritime trading networks and total isolation from Europe|The centralization of wealth and power shifting toward cooperative trading houses rather than solitary monarchs|The immediate abolition of traditional titles and secret societies|The complete cessation of internal African slavery and domestic labor systems|Option B|The palm oil trade required large-scale cooperative labor and canoe transportation, strengthening the Canoe House system and shifting wealth accumulation toward successful merchant chiefs.
2.1|In the context of the Niger Delta Canoe House System, what was the local term used to refer to a Canoe House?|Olofa|Wari|Ogiso|Imo|Option B|Wari is the indigenous term for a Canoe House, operating as a corporate household responsible for trade, social welfare, and defense.
2.1|Why did European merchants prefer dealing with the Canoe House system rather than individual traders during the legitimate commerce era?|Canoe Houses offered centralized credit reliability and efficient bulk collection of palm oil|Canoe Houses had no internal hierarchy and negotiated lower prices|Canoe Houses prohibited foreign currencies completely|Canoe Houses operated exclusively on barter systems without contracts|Option A|The corporate structure of the Canoe House provided collective accountability, creditworthiness, and the ability to aggregate large quantities of palm oil for European trading vessels.
2.1|Which of the following best describes the political relationship between the Amanyanabo and the individual Canoe House heads?|Absolute autocracy with total suppression of merchant autonomy|Decentralized corporate governance where powerful house heads wielded significant political leverage|Direct colonial governance managed by appointed European officials|Egalitarian communalism with no recognized political stratification|Option B|While the Amanyanabo held royal status, power was significantly decentralized, and wealthy Canoe House heads wielded substantial political and economic influence within the city-state.
2.1|What external economic factor primarily drove the transition from the slave trade to palm oil commerce in West Africa?|The Industrial Revolution in Europe creating a high demand for machine lubricants|The sudden depletion of all agricultural resources in the West African interior|The total ban on maritime navigation imposed by transatlantic powers|The discovery of vast gold reserves in the coastal riverbeds|Option A|The European Industrial Revolution created an urgent demand for vegetable oils to lubricate heavy industrial machinery, directly driving the shift to palm oil commerce.

4.1|What primary socio-political function does the Umunna lineage institution serve in traditional Igbo administration|Serving as the supreme judicial court for foreign diplomacy|Acting as the foundational family lineage unit that handles local governance and social security|Coordinating the absolute taxation of neighboring communities|Controlling the standing national military forces|Option B|The Umunna represents the extended family lineage group that forms the bedrock of social security, dispute resolution, and local administration in Igbo communities.
4.1|Who traditionally holds the sacred Ofo staff of authority within the foundational family lineage unit|The wealthy merchant guild leader|The younger warrior champion|The eldest male head known as the Okpara|The high priest of the earth deity Ala exclusively|Option C|The Okpara is the senior male head of the lineage who acts as the custodian of the sacred Ofo staff, symbolizing truth, justice, and ancestral authority.
4.1|What is the structural composition of the Oha-na-eze institution in traditional Igbo governance|An exclusive council of wealthy titled noblemen only|A democratic assembly comprising all adult males of the village|A secret tribunal of ritual medicine men|A restricted delegation of female elders only|Option B|The Oha-na-eze functions as a broad village assembly where all adult males gather to deliberate and achieve direct consensus on matters affecting the community.

4.1|How does the Ozo or Nze title society contribute to community governance in Igbo land|By enforcing hereditary monarchical succession laws|By providing a system of recognized personal integrity, leadership prestige, and judicial balance|By serving as a military cavalry unit during wartime|By managing external diplomatic relations with European powers|Option B|The Ozo or Nze title society is attained through merit and wealth criteria to validate personal integrity and enhance leadership credibility within the community.
4.1|What are the primary responsibilities traditionally assigned to Age Grades known as Uke or Ogbo|Conducting religious sacrifices to minor river gods|Executing public works, community development, and enforcing social discipline|Drafting written constitutions for the village assembly|Selecting candidates for hereditary kingship positions|Option B|Age grades act as the active workforce and security arm of the community, shouldering responsibilities for public works, infrastructure maintenance, and law enforcement.
4.1|What distinct administrative role does the Umuada perform as an assembly of daughters in traditional Igbo society|Acting as a powerful peace-making and conflict-resolution body in lineage matters|Functioning as the exclusive legislature for passing tax laws|Holding permanent military command over village defense forces|Ruling as absolute monarchs over market squares|Option A|The Umuada comprises daughters of the lineage who wield significant moral and political influence as neutral arbiters capable of intervening effectively in family and community disputes.
4.1|Which descriptive term best characterizes the structural arrangement of traditional Igbo political systems rather than a centralized state|Feudal hierarchy|Acephalous democracy|Imperial bureaucracy|Totalitarian autocracy|Option B|Traditional Igbo society is widely studied as an acephalous or headless democracy because power is dispersed among various institutions and assemblies rather than concentrated in a single monarch.
4.1|Why is consensus building considered vital in the legislative processes of traditional Igbo assemblies like Oha-na-eze|Majoritarian voting creates permanent minority factions that violate communal harmony|Direct consensus ensures that decisions command universal moral legitimacy without relying on coercive state machinery|Unanimous votes are legally mandated by colonial administrators|Majority voting is reserved strictly for religious rituals rather than politics|Option B|Because traditional Igbo governance lacks a centralized coercive apparatus or standing police force, policy decisions must achieve widespread consensus to secure voluntary compliance and preserve unity.

7.1|Which of the following best describes the structural triad of the Indirect Rule system implemented by the British in Nigeria?|Native Authority, Native Courts, and Native Treasury|Legislative Council, Executive Council, and Provincial Courts|Customs Service, Police Force, and Judicial Service|Governor-General, Lieutenant-Governors, and District Officers|Option A|Indirect Rule relied on the Native Authority system, Native Courts for local justice, and a Native Treasury to manage local taxation and expenditures.

7.1|What was the major constitutional innovation introduced by Sir Arthur Richards in the 1946 Constitution?|The formal establishment of a federal structure with regional civil services|The complete removal of British officials from the Executive Council|The introduction of regionalism through the division of the country into Northern, Western, and Eastern regions|The creation of universal adult suffrage across all provinces|Option C|The Richards Constitution of 1946 formally introduced regionalism into Nigerian administrative history by establishing regional councils for the North, West, and East to promote unity and greater participation.

7.1|What distinct administrative feature characterized the Lyttelton Constitution of 1954?|It dissolved all regional governments and created a unitary state|It established formal federalism and provided for distinct regional civil services|It introduced universal adult suffrage for the first time throughout the country|It ended all British oversight and declared complete national independence|Option B|The Lyttelton Constitution of 1954 marked the definitive shift to formal federalism, clearly delineating powers between the federal center and the regions, including the creation of regional public services.

11.1|What fundamental institutional shift characterized Nigeria's transition from the 1963 Constitution to the 1979 Presidential Constitution?|Adoption of the American Executive Presidential system combining Head of State and Head of Government roles|Retention of the British Westminster parliamentary model with a ceremonial president and executive prime minister|Establishment of a unitary government structure that abolished state legislatures and regional autonomy|Complete elimination of the judiciary branch in favor of military tribunals for all civil disputes|Option A|The 1979 Constitution marked a departure from the Westminster system to the American Executive Presidential model where the president serves as both Head of State and Head of Government.
11.1|Under the 1979 Presidential Constitution of Nigeria, how was executive power structured compared to the preceding Westminster system?|Concentrated exclusively within a prime minister who answered solely to the monarchy|Fused between a ceremonial head of state and a powerful legislative cabinet|Separated and vested in an executive president who operated independently of legislative tenure|Shared equally among a triumvirate of regional governors and a supreme military commander|Option C|Unlike the Westminster system where executive power was fused with the legislature through a prime minister, the 1979 Constitution created a distinct executive president independent of legislative tenure.
11.1|Which constitutional doctrine forms the bedrock of the 1979 Presidential Constitution regarding the allocation of governmental powers?|Fusion of powers ensuring absolute parliamentary supremacy over judicial decisions|Separation of powers distributing functions among the Executive National Assembly and Judiciary|Delegation of all administrative authority to traditional rulers and local government councils|Centralization of legislative and executive functions within a single ruling political party bureau|Option B|The 1979 Constitution introduced a strict separation of powers doctrine dividing responsibilities among the Executive, the National Assembly, and the Judiciary to prevent tyranny.
11.1|What was the primary constitutional purpose of introducing the Federal Character Principle in the 1979 Constitution?|To ensure equitable representation and prevent the domination of government by few states or ethnic groups|To centralize tax collection exclusively under the federal ministry of finance and economic planning|To mandate the rotation of the presidency among traditional emirs and regional kings every four years|To abolish state boundaries and create a unified administrative structure governed from Lagos|Option A|The Federal Character Principle was designed to promote national unity and belonging by ensuring public institutions reflected the diverse linguistic and geographic makeup of Nigeria.
11.1|How did the 1979 Constitution attempt to transform political parties from regional factions into national institutions?|By prohibiting political parties from registering unless they demonstrated a strict national spread in membership and leadership|By funding only the two largest political parties directly from the federal consolidated revenue fund annually|By restricting party membership exclusively to civil servants and retired military personnel with federal experience|By banning all forms of political campaigning outside the federal capital territory of Abuja|Option A|To prevent the recurrence of ethnically fractured regional parties, the 1979 Constitution required political parties to prove a broad national spread in both membership and organizational structure.
11.1|In the context of the 1979 Nigerian Executive Presidential system, what dual role is performed by the President?|Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces and Chief Justice of the Supreme Court одновременно|Head of State and Head of Government simultaneously|Sole legislator and chief auditor of federal accounts|Prime Minister and President of the Senate concurrently|Option B|The American-style executive presidency adopted in 1979 combined the ceremonial duties of Head of State with the executive administrative powers of Head of Government into a single office.
11.1|Which legislative body was established by the 1979 Constitution to replace the parliamentary legislature of the First Republic?|A unicameral parliament appointed directly by the federal executive council|A bicameral National Assembly consisting of the Senate and the House of Representatives|A Supreme Council of Elders and traditional rulers acting as the sole lawmaking authority|A regional assembly composed of delegates from all state civil service commissions|Option B|The 1979 Constitution established a bicameral National Assembly comprising a Senate and a House of Representatives to ensure federal representation and legislative checks.
11.1|What significant weakness of the Westminster parliamentary model did the drafters of the 1979 Constitution seek to avoid?|The lack of clear separation between the executive and the legislature leading to instability and mutual distrust|The excessive independence of the judiciary from political influence and public accountability|The absence of any provision for regional governments or local administrative units|The total exclusion of civilian politicians from matters concerning national defense and foreign policy|Option A|The Westminster model suffered from a fused executive and legislature which critics argued contributed to political instability during the First Republic, prompting the switch to a presidential system.
11.1|Which constitutional requirement was explicitly enforced to ensure that a winning presidential candidate enjoyed broad geographic support in 1979?|Securing a majority of total votes cast nationwide and a specific percentage of votes across at least two-thirds of all states|Winning unanimous endorsement from all traditional councils operating within the federation|Obtaining the highest number of votes in the federal capital territory regardless of state performance|Reaching a total of ninety percent voter turnout in every designated geo-political zone|Option A|To prevent sectional election victories, the 1979 Constitution required a winning presidential candidate to secure both a national majority and a constitutionally mandated spread across two-thirds of the states.
11.1|What structural impact did the 1979 Presidential Constitution have on the relationship between the executive branch and the legislature?|It created an institutional framework of checks and balances where neither branch could dissolve the other before its term expired|It subordinated the legislature entirely to executive decrees issued by the president during peacetime|It allowed the president to serve concurrently as a voting member of the National Assembly|It rendered the legislature completely powerless to review executive appointments or budgetary proposals|Option A|The presidential system established separate origins and survival for the executive and legislature, instituting checks and balances without the power of dissolution inherent in parliamentary systems.

1.1|Which fundamental political distinction separates pre-colonial Nigerian societies into cephalous and acephalous structures?|The presence or absence of a centralized, hierarchical authority and institutionalized state apparatus|The practice of nomadic pastoralism versus sedentary agricultural production|The adoption of external legal codes versus indigenous customary laws|The dominance of matrilineal succession over patrilineal inheritance systems|Option A|Cephalous societies feature centralized systems with kings or emirs, whereas acephalous societies lack a single centralized head and operate through segmentary lineage systems.
1.1|How did acephalous societies like the Igbo and Tiv traditionally manage political organization and social cohesion?|Through decentralized segmentary lineage systems and diffuse authority distributed among elders, age-grades, and title holders|Through an absolute monarchy supported by a standing royal army and taxation bureau|Through an overarching imperial bureaucracy commanded by appointed provincial governors|Through a military dictatorship sustained by external conquest and tribute collection|Option A|Acephalous societies lacked centralized kingships, relying instead on kinship groups, councils of elders, and age-grade associations to maintain social order.
1.1|What primary mechanism legitimized political authority and secured obedience within pre-colonial centralized Nigerian kingdoms and empires?|Sacred monarchy combined with religious rituals, ancestral lineage, and customary taboos|Strict adherence to written democratic constitutions and periodic popular elections|Bureaucratic accountability enforced by an independent judiciary and civil service commission|Economic redistribution driven by industrial capitalism and free-market forces|Option A|Centralized authorities derived their legitimacy from sacred kingship, divine or ancestral rights, and deeply embedded religious taboos that commanded reverence.
1.1|Which of the following best characterizes the structural nature of non-centralized pre-colonial administrative systems in Nigeria?|Segmentary and acephalous governance where political power is diffused across kindred groups and communal assemblies|Unified autocratic rule concentrated entirely within the office of a single paramount ruler|Feudal vassal states subservient to a central caliphate administration|A parliamentary confederation of city-states governed by elected magistrates|Option A|Acephalous or non-centralized societies are segmentary, meaning political power is distributed horizontally among various kinship segments rather than concentrated vertically.
1.1|In the study of pre-colonial Nigerian administrative history, what does the term cephalous denote?|Societies possessing a centralized political structure with defined governmental leadership such as kingdoms or empires|Societies organized strictly around migratory trading guilds without permanent territorial boundaries|Communities governed exclusively by religious clerics without any secular military defense|Populations practicing communal land ownership with absolute egalitarian economic distribution|Option A|Cephalous literally means having a head, which in administrative history refers to societies with a centralized head of state and institutionalized authority.
1.1|Which source of authority was predominantly relied upon to enforce social norms, laws, and political compliance in traditional Nigerian societies?|Customary taboos, ancestral heritage, and spiritual rituals deeply rooted in community worldview|Codified penal statutes enacted by a bicameral legislature and enforced by modern police forces|International maritime law ratified by neighboring sovereign nation-states|Corporate governance codes established by merchant trading monopolies|Option A|Pre-colonial governance relied heavily on tradition, ancestral legitimacy, and customary taboos rather than written statutory codes.
1.1|What distinguishes the political framework of the Sokoto Caliphate or the Oyo Empire from that of traditional Igbo or Tiv communities?|The presence of a highly centralized administrative hierarchy with delegated provincial rulers and judicial kadis or chiefs|An absence of any formal mechanisms for dispute resolution or community defense|A complete reliance on direct democracy through town-hall referendums for every decision|The total exclusion of religious ideology from matters of state administration and lawmaking|Option A|Centralized empires like Oyo or the Sokoto Caliphate utilized hierarchical administrative machineries, contrasting sharply with the decentralized structures of Igbo and Tiv societies.
1.1|How did ancestral lineage function as a basis of authority in pre-colonial Nigerian social organization?|It validated political office holding, land rights, and leadership succession based on proximity to the founding lineage|It served exclusively as an economic registry for trade tariff collections and market taxes|It determined military draft quotas for foreign imperial expansion campaigns|It functioned as a passport system for traveling between rival kingdoms and empires|Option A|Ancestral lineage established legitimate claims to political leadership and stewardship over communal land because authority was viewed as a sacred trust passed down from forebears.
1.1|What role did religious rituals play in sustaining political authority across pre-colonial Nigerian societies?|They reinforced political legitimacy by binding civic obedience to spiritual obligations and fear of supernatural sanctions|They functioned purely as recreational festivals devoid of any political or administrative significance|They were used exclusively to calculate agricultural crop yields and seasonal tax assessments|They served as diplomatic treaties signed between rival colonial trading partners|Option A|Religious rituals tied governance to the cosmos, making disobedience to authority not just a legal offense but a spiritual transgression against ancestors and deities.

1.1|What primary characteristic defines cephalous systems of governance in the context of pre-colonial Nigerian administrative history?|The presence of a centralized authority structure, institutionalized hierarchies, and formal leadership|The complete absence of any established laws, customs, or societal regulations|A purely nomadic lifestyle with zero permanent settlements or territorial boundaries|An egalitarian democratic framework where all community decisions require unanimous consensus|Option A|Cephalous systems are characterized by a centralized political authority, structured administrative machinery, and recognized ruling institutions like kingdoms and empires.

11.1|Under the 1979 Presidential Constitution of Nigeria, how were the roles of Head of State and Head of Government structured?|They were fused into a single office held by the elected executive president|They were divided between a ceremonial president and an executive prime minister|They were shared equally between the Senate President and the executive president|They were vested exclusively in the military high command while civilians managed legislation|Option A|Unlike the Westminster system where these roles were split, the executive presidential system fused both the Head of State and Head of Government into the president.

1.1|What is the defining structural feature of an acephalous society in the context of pre-colonial Nigerian history?|Absence of a centralized, hierarchical ruling authority or single head of state|Total reliance on foreign trade tariffs for state sustenance|Strict adherence to an Islamic caliphate legal code|Mandatory military conscription for all adult male citizens|Option A|Acephalous or non-centralized societies lack a centralized apex authority or king, relying instead on kinship, lineage, and decentralized councils.

11.1|Which governance model served as the primary blueprint for the executive structure introduced by the 1979 Nigerian Constitution?|The British Westminster parliamentary model|The French Fifth Republic semi-presidential model|The American Executive Presidential model|The Soviet collective leadership model|Option C|The framers of the 1979 Constitution deliberately looked to the United States to model their new executive presidential framework.

1.1|What is the primary defining characteristic of an acephalous society in the context of pre-colonial Nigerian administration?|The complete absence of a centralized, overarching tier of government and sovereign ruler|A system of government strictly controlled by an elected parliament and prime minister|A political framework dominated by an absolute monarch backed by a standing army|An administrative arrangement managed entirely by external colonial governors|Option A|Acephalous or non-centralized societies, such as the Igbo and Tiv, operated without a single centralized ruling authority or supreme sovereign.

1.1|How was political and administrative authority primarily legitimized in centralized pre-colonial Nigerian kingdoms?|Through sacred monarchy, religious rituals, and customary taboos|Through universal adult suffrage and periodic secret ballot elections|Through constitutional codification enforced by an independent judiciary|Through merit-based civil service examinations and bureaucratic appointments|Option A|Centralized kingdoms derived their legitimacy and social control from sacred monarchy, ancestral lineage, religious rituals, and deeply respected customary taboos.
1.1|What structural term is frequently used by political historians to describe centralized pre-colonial Nigerian systems with established monarchies?|Cephalous systems|Acephalous systems|Segmentary republics|Diffuse democracies|Option A|Cephalous systems refer to political entities possessing a head, capital, or centralized ruling authority, contrasting with acephalous systems.
1.1|Which mechanism served as a crucial instrument for maintaining social order and moral compliance in both centralized and non-centralized pre-colonial communities?|Customary taboos and ancestral lineage systems|Standardized penal codes drafted by a national legislature|International human rights conventions monitored by global tribunals|Standing mercenary armies deployed to enforce tax collection|Option A|Customary taboos, ancestral heritage, and religious sanctions acted as foundational mechanisms for maintaining law, order, and behavioral compliance without modern police forces.
1.1|The Sokoto Caliphate represents which broad administrative category of pre-colonial Nigerian history?|A centralized political structure|A non-centralized acephalous community|A segmentary lineage democracy|A stateless pastoral confederation|Option A|The Sokoto Caliphate was a highly organized, centralized administrative structure governed by Islamic political principles under the Emirs and the Caliph.
1.1|What role did religious rituals play in the administrative authority of pre-colonial Nigerian systems?|They reinforced political legitimacy and social cohesion by binding the spiritual and temporal realms|They served exclusively as commercial transactions to fund foreign trade expeditions|They were used by citizens to overthrow traditional rulers without consequence|They acted as formal legal petitions submitted to secular civil courts|Option A|Religious rituals deeply reinforced the authority of rulers and community leaders by validating their office through divine or ancestral approval.

1.1|Which of the following best defines a cephalous or centralized pre-colonial administrative system in Nigeria?|A society characterized by dispersed kinship groups with no standing political hierarchy|An empire or kingdom possessing a formal, hierarchical apparatus of government and centralized authority|A purely nomadic community governed temporarily by military conscription|An acephalous community where political decisions are made exclusively through open democratic town halls|Option B|Centralized (cephalous) systems feature structured, hierarchical ruling authorities like kingdoms, empires, and caliphates rather than fragmented governance.
1.1|What primary characteristic distinguishes acephalous societies from centralized kingdoms in pre-colonial Nigeria?|The absolute absence of any social control mechanisms or laws|The reliance on a single autocratic monarch with divine rights|The absence of a centralized, overarching political authority, often organized through segmentary lineages|The permanent presence of a standing colonial army to maintain internal peace|Option C|Acephalous (non-centralized) societies like the Igbo and Tiv operate via segmentary lineage systems without a single centralized governing hierarchy.
1.1|In pre-colonial centralized Nigerian societies, authority was frequently legitimized through which of the following mechanisms?|Universal adult suffrage and secret ballot elections|Written constitutions drafted by elected representatives|Sacred monarchy, ancestral lineage, and religious rituals|Strict adherence to imported foreign legal codes|Option C|Centralized political structures heavily relied on sacred monarchies, ancestral lines, customary taboos, and religious rituals to maintain legitimacy and social order.
1.1|Which of the following pre-colonial Nigerian groups is classic for exhibiting an acephalous or non-centralized administrative structure?|The old Oyo Empire|The Sokoto Caliphate|The Igbo and Tiv societies|The Benin Kingdom|Option C|The Igbo and Tiv are classic examples of acephalous (non-centralized) segmentary societies that managed affairs without a central monarchy.
1.1|How did non-centralized societies in pre-colonial Nigeria typically manage social and administrative cohesion?|Through hierarchical bureaucratic ministries and civil servants|Through segmentary lineage systems, age grades, and customary norms|Through imperial decrees issued by a supreme ruler|Through centralized tax collection agencies and standing police forces|Option B|Acephalous societies maintained order and governance through decentralized structures such as kinship ties, age grades, and customary laws rather than a central monarch.
1.1|Which concept best describes a political system where the king or ruler is viewed as divine or possessing sacred spiritual status?|Constitutional democracy|Sacred monarchy|Bureaucratic oligarchy|Direct federalism|Option B|Sacred monarchy is a form of governance where the ruler's authority is deeply intertwined with religious sanctity, rituals, and divine sanction.
1.1|What role did customary taboos and religious rituals play in pre-colonial Nigerian administrative systems?|They served merely as artistic performances with no political weight|They acted as powerful mechanisms of social control and legitimized political authority|They were imposed exclusively by foreign traders to regulate commerce|They functioned as written tax laws for the central treasury|Option C|Customary taboos and rituals reinforced law, order, and political compliance by embedding governance within the spiritual framework of the community.
1.1|Which term describes a society divided into equivalent, self-contained segments or lineages that unite for common defense or administrative needs?|Unitary state|Segmentary society|Feudal protectorate|Plutocratic corporation|Option B|Segmentary societies are acephalous communities structured around kinship segments that operate collectively without a permanent central government.
1.1|What was a primary structural difference between the Sokoto Caliphate and traditional Igbo political organization?|The Sokoto Caliphate was decentralized, whereas Igbo society was a centralized empire|The Sokoto Caliphate featured centralized hierarchical administration, whereas Igbo society was acephalous and segmentary|Both societies operated under identical monarchical structures with hereditary kings|Both societies relied strictly on nomadic councils without permanent settlements|Option B|The Sokoto Caliphate represents a centralized administrative structure, whereas traditional Igbo governance is acephalous and segmentary.

6.1|Which prominent body of kingmakers in the traditional Benin administrative structure consists of seven powerful nobles led by the Oliha?|The Eghaevbo n'Ore|The Eghaevbo n'Ogbe|The Uzama N'Ihinron|The Iwebo society|Option C|The Uzama N'Ihinron are the seven traditional kingmakers of the Benin Empire, headed by the Oliha, who play a vital constitutional role in installing the Oba.
6.1|What primary function is historically assigned to the Eghaevbo n'Ore in the governance of the Benin Empire?|Managing the private royal harem and royal domestic affairs|Acting as town chiefs who represent public interests and check royal power|Handling palace regalia and keeping sacred royal treasures|Serving exclusively as military commanders during foreign conquests|Option B|The Eghaevbo n'Ore are the town chiefs led by the Iyase, functioning as a vital administrative counterweight to check the absolute power of the Oba.
6.1|Who historically serves as the recognized leader and spokesperson for the Eghaevbo n'Ore (Town Chiefs) in the Benin administrative system?|The Oliha|The Iyase|The Eholo N'Ire|The Esogban|Option B|The Iyase serves as the leader of the Eghaevbo n'Ore and acts as the prime minister or primary voice of the town chiefs in government affairs.
6.1|Which of the three orders of chiefs in the Benin Kingdom is specifically responsible for managing palace administration and the royal household?|The Uzama N'Ihinron|The Eghaevbo n'Ore|The Eghaevbo n'Ogbe|The Ilesha council|Option C|The Eghaevbo n'Ogbe are the palace chiefs who manage the day-to-day administrative affairs within the royal court and palace grounds.
6.1|Within the Eghaevbo n'Ogbe palace administration, which specific society is tasked with the custodianship of the royal regalia and coronation paraphernalia?|The Iwebo|The Ibiwe|The Iweguae|The Uzama|Option A|The Iwebo society within the palace chiefs is traditionally responsible for the safekeeping, maintenance, and presentation of the Oba's royal regalia.
6.1|What specific jurisdiction is traditionally managed by the Ibiwe society within the palace administrative structure of the Benin Empire?|The public town markets and civil disputes|The personal royal harem and associated domestic staff|The physical royal treasury and monetary wealth|The external defense alliances and foreign diplomacy|Option B|The Ibiwe palace chiefs hold administrative charge over the royal harem and oversee the domestic quarters of the palace.
6.1|Which palace society among the Eghaevbo n'Ogbe is primarily entrusted with attending to the intimate personal needs and royal staff of the Oba?|The Iwebo|The Ibiwe|The Iweguae|The Uzama N'Ihinron|Option C|The Iweguae society is the palace group directly responsible for the personal attendants, private chambers, and royal staff serving the Oba.
6.1|How does the structural division of the Three Orders of Chiefs contribute to political stability in the historical Benin administrative system?|By concentrating all legislative and executive powers solely in the hands of the Oba|By creating a system of checks and balances among kingmakers, town chiefs, and palace officials|By abolishing hereditary titles in favor of merit-based annual appointments|By separating military functions entirely from any civil administrative participation|Option B|The division into the Uzama, town chiefs (Eghaevbo n'Ore), and palace chiefs (Eghaevbo n'Ogbe) established a sophisticated system of checks and balances that prevented autocratic overreach.

5.1|Which administrative official was specifically tasked with overseeing the administration and governance of the capital city within an emirate?|Galadima|Hakimi|Dagachi|Dogari|Option A|The Galadima was the designated official responsible for the direct administration and management of the capital city.
5.1|What specific responsibility did the Alkali hold within the judicial framework of the Sokoto Caliphate administration?|Administering and adjudicating cases according to Sharia law|Collecting annual agricultural and cattle taxes from nomads|Commanding the police force and maintaining public security|Managing the royal palace staff and protocol matters|Option A|The Alkali functioned as the Sharia judge responsible for resolving legal disputes and administering justice under Islamic law.
5.1|Which taxation system was specifically levied on cattle herders during the Hausa/Fulani administrative era under the Sokoto Caliphate?|Jangali|Jizyah|Kharaj|Zakat|Option A|Jangali was the traditional livestock or cattle tax specifically imposed on nomadic herdsmen within the emirate administrative framework.
