5.1|Which administrative title designated the head of the palace staff and internal court affairs in a traditional emirate?|Sarkin Fada|Sarkin Ruwa|Sarkin Pawa|Dogari|Option A|The Sarkin Fada was the senior official responsible for managing palace affairs, court protocols, and domestic palace administration.
5.1|What designated law enforcement function was performed by the Dogari within the pre-colonial Sokoto Caliphate administrative system?|Acting as traditional police to maintain law and order|Serving as the official tax collector for agricultural yields|Acting as the primary Islamic judge for civil disputes|Commanding the cavalry units during external military campaigns|Option A|The Dogari served as the traditional police force responsible for enforcing orders, maintaining public security, and supporting the judicial system.
7.1|What was the primary economic motivation behind the 1914 amalgamation of Northern and Southern Nigeria by Lord Frederick Lugard?|To merge the profitable Northern railway with the bankrupt Southern administration for financial self-sufficiency|To establish a unified currency and banking system across West Africa|To create a massive tax base to fund British military campaigns in Europe|To centralize agricultural exports specifically for the French trade market|Option A|The Northern protectorate ran a budget deficit while the South had a surplus and thriving railways, prompting Lugard to merge them for administrative and financial convenience.|
7.1|Which of the following triad pillars formed the foundational infrastructure of Lord Lugard's Indirect Rule system?|Native Authority Native Courts and Native Treasury|Legislative Council Executive Council and Civil Service Commission|Provincial Courts District Officers and Paramilitary Police Forces|Emirs Obas and Warrant Chiefs ruling independently without oversight|Option A|Indirect rule operated through traditional structures reorganized into Native Authorities, Native Courts for justice, and Native Treasuries for local revenue collection.|
7.1|Why did the Indirect Rule system experience catastrophic failure in Eastern Nigeria?|The imposition of Warrant Chiefs violated egalitarian Igbo political structures leading to the Aba Women's War|The local population completely rejected British currency in favor of traditional cowries|The Islamic legal system introduced by British administrators conflicted with indigenous traditions|The region lacked navigable rivers making communication impossible for British residents|Option A|Unlike the North and West, the Igbo lacked centralized leadership, making the imposition of Warrant Chiefs artificial and deeply resented, culminating in the 1929 Aba Women's War.|
7.1|Which landmark constitutional development introduced the elective principle for the first time in Nigeria's history?|Clifford Constitution of 1922|Richards Constitution of 1946|Macpherson Constitution of 1951|Lyttelton Constitution of 1954|Option A|The Clifford Constitution of 1922 introduced the elective principle, allowing a limited number of Africans to be elected into the Legislative Council and paving the way for Herbert Macaulay's NNDP.|
7.1|What was the most significant structural innovation of the Richards Constitution of 1946?|It laid the foundation for regionalism by dividing the country into Northern, Western, and Eastern regions|It granted full independence to Nigeria under a parliamentary framework|It established a centralized unitary government that abolished traditional ruler councils|It created separate civil services for each of the federating regions immediately|Option A|Arthur Richards' 1946 constitution advanced regionalism by establishing regional councils for the North, West, and East, bridging the gap between central government and local administration.|
7.1|How did the Macpherson Constitution of 1951 alter Nigeria's constitutional trajectory?|It introduced a quasi-federal system that expanded regional legislative powers and established a central House of Representatives|It abolished the elective principle entirely in favor of appointed legislative delegates|It created the position of Prime Minister for the entire country for the first time|It severed all administrative ties between the Northern and Southern protectorates|Option A|The 1951 Macpherson Constitution established a quasi-federal structure, giving increased legislative autonomy and authority to the regional assemblies.|
7.1|Which constitutional milestone finally cemented Nigeria's status as a formal federation with distinct regional civil services?|Lyttelton Constitution of 1954|Clifford Constitution of 1922|Macpherson Constitution of 1951|Richards Constitution of 1946|Option A|The Lyttelton Constitution of 1954 established formal federalism and instituted separate civil services for the regions, addressing regional demands for autonomy.|
7.1|Which political party was formed in direct response to the introduction of the elective principle under the 1922 Clifford Constitution?|Nigerian National Democratic Party|National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons|Action Group|Northern Peoples Congress|Option A|Herbert Macaulay founded the Nigerian National Democratic Party in 1923 to contest the elective seats introduced by the Clifford Constitution of 1922.|
7.1|What fundamental administrative issue led to the outbreak of the 1929 Aba Women's War in southeastern Nigeria?|The threat of direct taxation imposed through unpopular Warrant Chiefs|The forced conscription of women into British colonial plantation labor|The banning of traditional religious festivals by British administrative officers|The confiscation of ancestral lands for railway construction projects|Option A|The resistance was sparked by fears that the British colonial administration intended to extend direct taxation to women via the unpopular Warrant Chiefs system.|
7.1|Under the Indirect Rule system, how were traditional rulers utilized by the British colonial administration?|As agents of local governance who collected taxes and maintained order under British supervision|As independent monarchs with absolute sovereign authority over foreign policy|As military commanders deployed to suppress rebellions in neighboring colonies|As ceremonial figures with no administrative or financial responsibilities whatsoever|Option A|Traditional rulers were co-opted as Native Authorities to implement colonial policies, collect taxes, and administer local native courts under the watchful eye of British officers.|

11.1|Under the 1979 Presidential Constitution of Nigeria, how was the office of the Chief Executive structured at the federal level?|The roles of Head of State and Head of Government were fused into a single executive president|The Prime Minister acted as Head of Government while a ceremonial President served as Head of State|Power was equally shared between a Chancellor and a Prime Minister|The Head of State position was rotated annually among regional governors|Option A|Unlike the Westminster system where the Head of State and Head of Government are separate, the 1979 presidential system combined both roles into a single Executive President.

1.1|What role did customary taboos and religious rituals play in pre-colonial administration?|They served as internal social control mechanisms to maintain law and order|They functioned as economic tariffs levied on foreign merchants|They acted as formal written constitutions defining state boundaries|They were military strategies utilized during territorial expansion wars|Option A|Customary taboos and religious rituals acted as powerful moral and social checks that regulated human behavior and maintained societal cohesion without requiring a massive standing police force.
1.1|Which structural feature was most prominent in the administration of centralized pre-colonial Nigerian states?|Hierarchical offices, subordinate chiefs, and institutionalized tribute systems|Egalitarian councils where every individual held equal executive power|Complete absence of taxation or compulsory labor obligations|Purely nomadic governance with shifting administrative capitals|Option A|Centralized systems required established hierarchies, including subordinate chiefs, titleholders, and mechanisms like tribute collection to sustain the central government.
1.1|What term best describes societies such as the old Oyo Empire or the Sokoto Caliphate in historical administrative studies?|Cephalous systems with structured administrative centers|Acephalous systems with fragmented lineage groups|Feudal democracies with universal suffrage|Stateless confederacies without permanent leadership|Option A|Cephalous societies are characterized by centralized political institutions, distinct capitals, and hierarchical governing structures.
1.1|In segmentary acephalous societies, political and social cohesion was primarily maintained through which of the following?|Kinship ties, clan affiliations, and age-grade associations|A centralized standing army controlled by a supreme chief|A codified body of penal laws enforced by royal judges|A centralized treasury collecting mandatory annual taxes|Option A|Without a centralized ruler, acephalous societies relied heavily on kinship bonds, councils of elders, and age-grade systems to resolve conflicts and manage community affairs.
1.1|The exercise of power in pre-colonial centralized administrations was heavily anchored on which concept?|Divine right of kings and ancestral sanction|Constitutional term limits and parliamentary checks|Secular humanism and separation of powers|Universal adult suffrage and popular sovereignty|Option A|Centralized systems like kingdoms and empires derived their authority largely from sacred monarchy and the belief in divine or ancestral sanction.
1.1|Which factor fundamentally distinguishes the governance structure of the Tiv people from that of the Hausa City-States?|The Tiv utilized a decentralized segmentary lineage system while the Hausa featured centralized monarchies|The Tiv practiced industrial capitalism whereas the Hausa relied purely on pastoralism|The Tiv had a single supreme emperor while the Hausa had no recognized leaders|The Tiv were governed by colonial fiat while the Hausa were entirely stateless|Option A|The Tiv represent acephalous segmentary organization, whereas the Hausa City-States developed advanced centralized monarchical and administrative structures.

12.1|What was a major structural innovation introduced by the Udoji Commission of 1974 to streamline public compensation?|Unified Grading and Salary Structure|Decentralized salary negotiation per ministry|Direct political appointment of directors|Restoration of permanent secretary career security|Option B|The Udoji Commission recommended the Unified Grading and Salary Structure (UGSS) to bridge gaps across different public service grades.
12.1|Which advanced management techniques were famously introduced into the Nigerian civil service by the Udoji Commission?|Management by Objectives and Program and Performance Budgeting System|Hierarchical centralization and strict bureaucratic red tape|Single-ministry professionalization and political accounting|Decentralized regional civil service commissions|Option A|Udoji introduced modern private-sector management tools like Management by Objectives (MBO) and Program and Performance Budgeting System (PPBS) to enhance efficiency.
12.1|Under the 1988 Babangida Civil Service Reform, who was designated as the Chief Executive and Accounting Officer of a ministry?|The Permanent Secretary|The Minister|The Director-General|The Head of the Civil Service|Option B|The 1988 reform shifted power by making the Minister both the political head, Chief Executive, and the Accounting Officer of the ministry.

12.1|What structural principle defined the civil service organization under the 1988 Babangida Reform based on the Phillips Report?|Single-ministry professionalization|Inter-ministerial fluid rotation of personnel|Regional autonomy for state branches|Comprehensive alignment with the Gorsuch model|Option A|The 1988 reform introduced single-ministry professionalization, requiring an officer to build their entire career within one ministry to develop deep expertise.
12.1|Which review panel was responsible for reversing the major structural changes introduced by the 1988 Babangida Civil Service Reform?|Ayida Panel 1997|Udoji Commission 1974|Gorsuch Commission 1954|Phillips Review Committee|Option A|The Ayida Panel of 1997 reviewed the 1988 reforms and recommended reversing several provisions to restore neutrality and institutional memory.
12.1|What key status regarding career civil servants was restored by the Ayida Panel of 1997?|Permanent career status of the Permanent Secretary|Political tenure for all executive directors|Unified salary structures across regional boards|Management by Objectives across all parastatals|Option A|The Ayida Panel restored the permanent career status of the Permanent Secretary, stripping away the political tenure tag introduced in 1988.
12.1|Which report served as the core analytical blueprint for the 1988 Babangida administrative reforms in Nigeria?|Phillips Report|Gorsuch Report|Udoji Report|Ayida Report|Option A|The Phillips Report provided the core intellectual and structural framework that guided the 1988 Babangida civil service restructuring.
12.1|How did the 1988 Babangida Reform alter the traditional designation of the administrative head of a ministry?|From Permanent Secretary to Director-General|From Minister to Permanent Secretary|From Director-General to Accounting Clerk|From Chairman to Minister-General|Option A|The 1988 reform formally changed the title of the administrative head from Permanent Secretary to Director-General, aligning it with a political tenure.

1.1|What primary mechanism legitimized political power and authority within centralized pre-colonial Nigerian monarchies?|Universal adult suffrage|Sacred monarchy and religious rituals|Democratic constitutionalism|Direct taxation without representation|Option B|Centralized states relied heavily on sacred kingship, ancestral lineage, and religious rituals to secure obedience and legitimize rulers.|
1.1|How was political authority predominantly structured in non-centralized Nigerian societies prior to colonial rule?|Through hereditary divine kings|Through decentralized lineage networks and age grades|Through an absolute central military dictator|Through appointed provincial governors|Option B|Non-centralized societies distributed administrative power across kinship ties, extended families, and age-grade associations rather than a single monarch.|
1.1|Which factor served as a vital social control mechanism reinforcing customary laws in pre-colonial Nigerian communities?|Written penal codes|Customary taboos and religious sanctions|International human rights treaties|Parliamentary legislation|Option B|Customary taboos and spiritual sanctions acted as powerful compliance tools to maintain order and respect for authority.|
1.1|The presence of hierarchical administrative machinery spanning vast territories is a defining feature of which administrative system?|Segmentary lineage systems|Acephalous confederations|Centralized kingdoms and empires|Stateless village republics|Option C|Centralized systems possessed structured institutional apparatuses capable of governing expansive geographical territories.|
1.1|In pre-colonial administrative analysis, what distinguishes segmentary societies from centralized states?|The complete absence of any social organization|The diffusion of political authority across equivalent segments rather than a single center|The reliance on imported European laws|The presence of a standing national army|Option B|Segmentary societies disperse authority among parallel lineages or clans instead of concentrating power in a central government.|
1.1|What role did ancestral lineage play in the administrative systems of pre-colonial Nigerian societies?|It was legally prohibited in public office|It determined social status, succession rights, and political authority|It was relevant only for economic trade guilds|It served solely religious functions independent of governance|Option B|Ancestral lineage dictated political succession, social hierarchy, and legitimacy in both centralized and non-centralized settings.|
1.1|Why is understanding the distinction between cephalous and acephalous systems crucial for studying pre-colonial Nigerian administration?|It proves that all Nigerian societies had identical governance structures|It highlights the diverse indigenous political adaptations and foundations of authority across different regions|It shows that non-centralized societies had no system of law whatsoever|It demonstrates that colonialism introduced the concept of authority for the first time|Option B|Recognizing these distinct systems reveals the rich political variety and indigenous mechanisms of social control present before colonial intervention.
2.1|Which primary historical shift characterized the evolution of Niger Delta city-states such as Bonny and Nembe during the pre-colonial era?|Transition from the transatlantic slave trade to legitimate commerce in palm oil|Shift from agricultural production to maritime fishing monopolies|Abandonment of coastal settlements for inland plateau trading posts|Dismantling of traditional monarchies in favor of military dictatorships|Option A|Niger Delta city-states transitioned from involvement in the transatlantic slave trade to legitimate commerce centered around palm oil.
2.1|What was the principal administrative and socio-political unit that organized trade and governance in the Niger Delta city-states?|The Canoe House System or Wari|The Age-Grade council of elders|The central imperial feudal domain|The nomadic pastoral confederation|Option A|The Canoe House System, known locally as Wari, served as the core socio-political and economic framework for trade and governance.
2.1|Who held supreme executive and economic authority at the head of a traditional Canoe House in the Niger Delta?|A merchant chief holding the title of Amanyanabo|An externally appointed British colonial governor|A spiritual high priest elected by the age grades|A rotating council of foreign European merchants|Option A|Merchant chiefs known as Amanyanabo served as the leaders of the Canoe Houses, directing trade fleets and domestic governance.
2.1|What role did secret societies like the Ekpe play within the administrative framework of the Niger Delta societies?|Enforcing commercial contracts and maintaining public order|Collecting direct property taxes on behalf of the British crown|Directing military expansion into neighboring savannah kingdoms|Regulating religious dogma and international maritime law|Option A|Secret societies such as Ekpe functioned as institutional mechanisms for enforcing contracts, regulating trade, and maintaining public order.
2.1|Which of the following specific coastal groups is explicitly recognized alongside Bonny, Nembe, and Kalabari in the development of Niger Delta city-states?|The Itsekiri people|The Hausa emirates|The Kanem-Borno empire|The Nupe kingdom|Option A|The Itsekiri are documented alongside Bonny, Nembe, and Kalabari as prominent coastal kingdoms engaged in regional trade and administration.
2.1|Why was the transition from the slave trade to palm oil commerce significant for Niger Delta administrative structures?|It required new organizational capacities to manage large-scale collection and processing through house units|It led to the immediate dissolution of all indigenous trading houses and chiefs|It forced city-states to abandon coastal waterways entirely for desert caravan routes|It replaced indigenous currencies with European paper tender overnight|Option A|The shift to palm oil necessitated complex logistical management within the Canoe House system to aggregate produce from hinterland suppliers.
2.1|In the context of the Niger Delta administrative history, what does the term Wari denote?|The indigenous Canoe House system used for commerce and social organization|A sacred grove reserved exclusively for coronating supreme kings|A defensive fortification built against European gunboats|An annual festival celebrating the yam harvest season|Option A|Wari is the local term for the Canoe House system, which functioned as both a trading corporation and a social governance unit.
2.1|How did the leadership of a Canoe House maintain discipline and economic productivity among its diverse members?|Through internal governance structures backed by the authority of the merchant chief and secret societies|Through mandatory military conscription into regional armies|Through permanent exile of unproductive members to foreign territories|Through direct judicial intervention by foreign colonial courts|Option A|Merchant chiefs and regulatory bodies like secret societies maintained strict discipline, contract enforcement, and operational efficiency within the houses.
2.1|What primary economic factor drove European powers and African city-states to embrace legitimate commerce in the nineteenth century?|The legal abolition of the transatlantic slave trade and rising industrial demand for vegetable oils|The complete exhaustion of all mineral resources in the West African interior|The sudden collapse of maritime shipping technology across the Atlantic basin|The signing of the Berlin Conference partitioning the entire Niger Delta|Option A|Industrialization in Europe created a massive demand for palm oil as a machine lubricant, replacing the slave trade.
2.1|Which of the following best describes the structural nature of the Niger Delta city-states during the legitimate commerce era?|Commercial oligarchies centered around corporate trading houses that mobilized labor and fleets|Absolute autocracies controlled by a single hereditary priest-king without council input|Egalitarian communes governed entirely through direct popular assemblies|Decentralized pastoral nomadic bands with no permanent urban settlements|Option A|The city-states operated largely as commercial oligarchies where wealthy merchant chiefs organized trade through corporate household structures.
13.1|Which key structural change was introduced by the nationwide 1976 Local Government Reform in Nigeria?|A multi-tiered regional government structure|A uniform single-tier system of local government|A decentralized federation of village councils|A dual-control system shared with colonial district officers|Option B|The 1976 reform dismantled heterogeneous structures by establishing a uniform single-tier system of local government across the country.
13.1|What major constitutional status did the 1976 Local Government Reform officially confer on local governments in Nigeria?|Recognition as the primary tier of government|Sub-units entirely dependent on regional ministries|Recognition as the third tier of government in the federal structure|Autonomous corporate entities separate from the federation|Option C|The 1976 reform structurally anchored local government as the third tier of government, establishing its legitimate place in Nigeria's governance framework.
13.1|How were traditional rulers positioned within local administration following the 1976 Local Government Reform?|They were granted full executive and legislative authority over local councils|They were completely abolished from any administrative or social role|They were insulated from partisan politics and restricted to advisory councils|They were appointed as permanent chief executive officers of the councils|Option C|To modernize administration and prevent partisan conflict, traditional rulers were insulated and assigned to advisory roles through traditional councils.
13.1|What financial mechanism was introduced by the 1976 reform to ensure financial viability for local governments?|Direct commercial taxation powers over multinational corporations|Statutory revenue allocation directly from the Federation Account|Voluntary annual grants donated by state governors|Exclusive rights to collect international customs duties|Option B|The 1976 reform guaranteed financial autonomy by instituting regular statutory revenue allocations flowing from the national Federation Account.
13.1|What was the primary administrative focus of the 1984 Dasuki Committee report regarding local government?|Reorganizing local government structure finances and roles|Transferring all local governance back to traditional emirs and chiefs|Abolishing elected councils in favor of military sole administrators|Merging local government councils with federal ministries of defense|Option A|The Dasuki Committee of 1984 was instituted to review and recommend improvements on the structure, finances, and operational efficiency of local governments.
13.1|Which structural leadership position was introduced for local government councils under the Babangida reforms of 1988?|Appointed Military Sole Administrators with veto powers|Executive Chairmen heading the local council executive branch|Permanent Secretaries representing the federal civil service|Elected traditional monarchs serving as ceremonial presidents|Option B|The 1988 reforms under Babangida professionalized local leadership by introducing Executive Chairmen to spearhead the executive branch of local councils.
13.1|What change regarding financial transfers was popularized during the Babangida reforms to empower local governance?|Direct revenue transfers bypassing arbitrary state government withholding|Revenue collection managed entirely by traditional rulers|Abolition of all federal grants to local administrative bodies|Mandatory funding through foreign international loans|Option A|The Babangida administration implemented direct revenue transfers to local governments, mitigating state-level bureaucratic delays and financial interference.
13.1|Which historical event or committee directly preceded the 1988 Babangida local government administrative reforms?|The Willink Commission of 1958|The Dasuki Committee of 1984|The Udoji Public Service Review Commission of 1974|The Morgan Commission of 1963|Option B|The 1984 Dasuki Committee recommendations served as the foundational blueprint for the structural changes implemented during the 1988 Babangida reforms.
13.1|Why were traditional rulers explicitly insulated from executive functions in the 1976 local government structure?|To reduce government spending on royal entitlements|To prevent political friction and preserve their dignity through advisory duties|To transition local governments into wholly commercial enterprises|To eliminate cultural heritage from public administration completely|Option B|Isolating traditional rulers into advisory councils protected their cultural prestige and prevented direct clashes with elected modern administrative officials.
13.1|Prior to the 1976 Local Government Reform, what characterized the structural arrangement of local administration across Nigeria?|A uniform single-tier system nationwide|Diverse, multi-tiered, and fragmented systems across different regions|Direct centralized rule by the federal military government without regions|Complete autonomy granted to village headmen without regional oversight|Option B|Before the 1976 reform standardized the system, Nigerian local government featured fragmented and heterogeneous multi-tiered structures varying widely across regions.
12.1|Which historical commission is credited with establishing the foundational four functional classes in the Nigerian civil service?|Gorsuch Commission 1954|Udoji Commission 1974|Ayida Panel 1997|Phillips Report 1988|Option A|The Gorsuch Commission of 1954 is historically known for structuring the civil service into four distinct functional classes to meet administrative needs.
12.1|What was a primary structural innovation introduced by the Udoji Commission of 1974 in Nigeria?|Unified Grading and Salary Structure|Professionalization of single ministries|Minister as the Chief Executive and Accounting Officer|Restoration of the Permanent Secretary title|Option A|The Udoji Commission recommended the Unified Grading and Salary Structure UGSS to harmonize salaries and grading across the public service.
12.1|Which modern management techniques were explicitly introduced into the Nigerian public administration by the Udoji Commission?|Management by Objectives and Planning Programming Budgeting System|Decentralized federalism and direct taxation|Military command structures and martial law administration|Absolute legislative supremacy and judicial review|Option A|The Udoji Commission introduced modern management tools such as Management by Objectives MBO and Planning Programming Budgeting System PPBS.
12.1|Under the 1988 Babangida Civil Service Reform based on the Phillips Report, who was designated as the Chief Executive and Accounting Officer of a ministry?|The Minister|The Permanent Secretary|The Director-General|The Head of Service|Option A|The 1988 reform altered traditional arrangements by making the Minister both the Chief Executive and the Accounting Officer of the ministry.
12.1|What significant structural change did the 1988 Babangida reform introduce regarding the tenure and designation of the administrative head of a ministry?|Director-General with political tenure|Permanent Secretary with career tenure|Auditor-General with judicial immunity|Sole Administrator with emergency powers|Option A|The 1988 reform replaced the permanent career post of Permanent Secretary with the political tenure post of Director-General.
12.1|What core principle of civil service professionalism was emphasized by the 1988 Babangida reform regarding an officer's career path?|Single-ministry professionalization|Inter-ministerial rotation and generalist deployment|Regional decentralization and local autonomy|Private sector secondment and corporate governance|Option A|The 1988 reform introduced single-ministry professionalization, requiring officers to spend their entire career within one ministry to acquire specialized expertise.
12.1|Which administrative review body was responsible for reversing the major structural changes of the 1988 Babangida reform in Nigeria?|Ayida Panel 1997|Gorsuch Commission 1954|Udoji Commission 1974|Morgan Commission 1963|Option A|The Ayida Panel of 1997 was established to review the civil service and subsequently recommended reversing the 1988 structural changes.
12.1|What was a principal outcome of the Ayida Panel of 1997 with respect to top bureaucratic leadership?|Restored the permanent career status of the Permanent Secretary|Retained the Minister as the sole Accounting Officer|Abolished the Unified Grading and Salary Structure completely|Reintroduced the four functional classes of 1954|Option A|The Ayida Panel restored the classic career title and permanent status of the Permanent Secretary, undoing the politicization of that office under the 1988 reform.
12.1|How did the 1988 Babangida reform differ from the Ayida Panel recommendations concerning ministerial leadership roles?|1988 made the Minister the Chief Executive while Ayida reinforced civil service neutrality and traditional bureaucratic roles|1988 abolished ministries while Ayida expanded them|1988 introduced MBO while Ayida abolished all budgeting systems|1988 established regional governance while Ayida created unitary rule|Option A|The 1988 reform centralized executive powers in the political minister, whereas the Ayida Panel sought to restore traditional bureaucratic equilibrium and neutrality.
12.1|Which administrative reform package introduced both sweeping structural alterations to political-bureaucratic roles and innovative management techniques like MBO?|Udoji Commission 1974 and Babangida Reform 1988|Gorsuch Commission 1954 only|Ayida Panel 1997 only|Morgan Commission 1963 and Gorsuch Commission 1954|Option A|The Udoji Commission introduced modern management techniques like MBO while the 1988 Babangida reform restructured political and administrative executive responsibilities.
3.1|Which traditional political institution in the Oyo Empire held supreme executive and monarchical authority at the central government level?|The Oyo Mesi|The Alaafin of Oyo|The Ogboni Society|The Aare Ona Kakanfo|Option B|The Alaafin of Oyo was the supreme monarch and head of the central government in the traditional Oyo administrative system.
3.1|What role did the Oyo Mesi play within the administrative structure of the old Oyo Empire?|They served as provincial tax collectors and resident governors|They acted as the supreme military commanders of the cavalry|They functioned as the council of seven kingmaker chiefs led by the Bashorun|They operated as the judicial tribunal for high treason cases|Option C|The Oyo Mesi were a council of seven prominent kingmaker chiefs headed by the Bashorun responsible for selecting and checking the Alaafin.
3.1|How did the traditional checks and balances system in the Oyo Empire deal with a tyrannical or abusive Alaafin?|Through impeachment and permanent exile to a foreign territory|By sending an empty calabash or parrot eggs to compel ritual suicide|By dissolving the council of chiefs and seizing royal assets|Through military coup d'état orchestrated by provincial governors|Option B|The delivery of an empty calabash or parrot eggs by the Oyo Mesi signified a loss of confidence and compelled the Alaafin to commit ritual suicide.
3.1|What was the primary function of the Ogboni society within the checks and balances mechanism of the Oyo Empire?|Acting as a spiritual and political mediator between the Alaafin and the Oyo Mesi|Commanding the elite Eso Ikoyi cavalry forces during wartime|Collecting tribute from conquered provincial towns and territories|Serving as the official tax monitoring body in distant provinces|Option A|The Ogboni society played a crucial stabilizing role by mediating conflicts and balancing the powers of the Alaafin and the Oyo Mesi.
3.1|Who were the Ajele in the administrative framework of the Oyo Empire?|Resident monitors and administrative agents sent to oversee provincial territories|The elite royal bodyguards guarding the inner chambers of the palace|Senior military generals commanding the imperial infantry divisions|Hereditary land-owning chiefs who advised the central government|Option A|The Ajele functioned as resident monitors or agents appointed by the central authority to oversee administration and tributes in the provinces.
3.1|What distinctive military designation was held by the commander-in-chief of the Oyo army who was required to achieve victory or face death?|Bashorun|Ajele|Aare Ona Kakanfo|Eso Ikoyi|Option C|The Aare Ona Kakanfo was the supreme military commander of the Oyo army, bound by tradition to either win all battles or die in combat.
3.1|How many elite military commanders made up the famous Eso Ikoyi warrior class in the Oyo military setup?|Twelve major warlords|Fifty royal guards|Seventy commanders|One hundred senior officers|Option C|The Eso Ikoyi comprised seventy elite military commanders who formed the backbone of the Oyo military defense and expansion.
3.1|Who led the council of seven kingmakers known as the Oyo Mesi?|The Aare Ona Kakanfo|The Bashorun|The Ajele|The Onpetu|Option B|The Bashorun served as the leader and spokesperson of the Oyo Mesi council of kingmaker chiefs.
3.1|Which body possessed the constitutional authority to reject a tyrannical monarch in the Oyo Empire before the ritual sanction was applied?|The Ogboni society|The Eso Ikoyi generals|The Aare Ona Kakanfo|The Oyo Mesi|Option D|The Oyo Mesi held the authority to reject a tyrannical Alaafin by presenting symbols that compelled his ritual suicide.
3.1|Which administrative tier was primarily responsible for managing external military defense and provincial oversight in the Oyo Empire?|The central palace administration only|The provincial and military apparatus including Ajele and the Aare Ona Kakanfo|The local village councils of elders exclusively|The religious priesthood of traditional deities|Option B|The provincial and military apparatus consisting of figures like the Ajele and the Aare Ona Kakanfo managed external security and territorial control.

7.1|What was the primary motivating factor behind the amalgamation of the Northern and Southern Protectorates in 1914 by Lord Frederick Lugard?|Ideological unification of diverse ethnic groups|Economic convenience and the integration of railway systems|Democratic pressure from indigenous nationalist movements|Implementation of a unified parliamentary system of government|Option B|The 1914 amalgamation was primarily driven by administrative and economic convenience, specifically to merge the financial resources of the wealthy South with the debt-ridden North and to coordinate railway infrastructure.
7.1|Which of the following was a core institutional pillar of Lord Lugard's Indirect Rule system in Nigeria?|Bicameral legislature|Native Authority, Native Courts, and Native Treasury|Universal adult suffrage and secret ballot elections|A centralized federal civil service spanning the entire territory|Option B|Indirect rule operated through traditional structures transformed into colonial instruments, fundamentally relying on the Native Authority, Native Courts, and Native Treasury.
7.1|Why did the Indirect Rule system experience catastrophic failure in the Eastern Provinces of Nigeria?|The region lacked any form of pre-existing traditional leadership structure|Traditional rulers rejected Western education completely|The imposition of Warrant Chiefs disrupted indigenous political systems and sparked the Aba Women's War|The British refused to establish Native Courts in the East|Option C|Unlike the North or West, the East was largely stateless or decentralized; appointing autocratic Warrant Chiefs ignored local customs and triggered intense resentment culminating in the 1929 Aba Women's War.
7.1|What major political innovation was introduced into British West Africa by the Clifford Constitution of 1922?|The establishment of formal federalism|The introduction of the elective principle which led to the formation of political parties like the NNDP|The creation of regional assemblies with legislative powers|Universal adult suffrage for all citizens|Option B|The Clifford Constitution of 1922 introduced the elective principle for the first time in British West Africa, enabling the election of representatives to the Legislative Council and inspiring Herbert Macaulay to found the NNDP.
7.1|Which constitutional framework officially introduced regionalism and laid the groundwork for regional assemblies in Nigeria?|The Clifford Constitution of 1922|The Richards Constitution of 1946|The Macpherson Constitution of 1951|The Lyttelton Constitution of 1954|Option B|The Richards Constitution of 1946 divided the country into Northern, Western, and Eastern regions, formally introducing regionalism into Nigerian constitutional development.
7.1|The Macpherson Constitution of 1951 is best described as which type of constitutional arrangement?|A unitary state with decentralized local authorities|A confederation of independent sovereign states|A quasi-federal constitution that increased regional autonomy while maintaining central legislative mechanisms|A purely ceremonial monarchy with no executive powers|Option C|The 1951 Macpherson Constitution established a quasi-federal structure that expanded regional legislative and executive powers while retaining a central legislative body.
7.1|Which constitution finally established a formal federal system of government and regionalized the civil services in Nigeria?|The Clifford Constitution of 1922|The Richards Constitution of 1946|The Macpherson Constitution of 1951|The Lyttelton Constitution of 1954|Option D|The Lyttelton Constitution of 1954 established formal federalism in Nigeria, clearly demarcating powers between the federal center and the regions, including the regionalization of civil services.
7.1|How did the application of Indirect Rule vary across the three major regions of Nigeria during the colonial era?|It succeeded universally across all regions without any resistance|It succeeded in the North, met partial success in the West, and failed in the East|It failed completely in the North due to strong Islamic opposition but succeeded in the East|It was never implemented outside of Lagos Colony|Option B|Indirect rule thrived where centralized hierarchical authorities already existed (North and parts of West), but failed in the decentralized societies of the East.
7.1|What was a direct consequence of the administrative integration of the Lagos Colony with the Northern and Southern Protectorates in 1914?|The immediate granting of independence to Nigeria|The creation of a unified colonial territory administered under Lord Frederick Lugard as Governor-General|The dissolution of all traditional monarchies in the Southern Protectorate|The adoption of a presidential system of government modeled after the United States|Option B|The 1914 amalgamation brought the Lagos Colony and the two protectorates under a single centralized administration headed by Governor-General Lord Frederick Lugard.

11.1|What fundamental institutional shift characterized Nigeria's transition from the First Republic to the 1979 Constitution?|Adoption of the French semi-presidential model|Transition from the British Westminster parliamentary system to the American-style executive presidential system|Merging of the judiciary and the executive branches into a single supreme council|Establishment of a unitary government with absolute legislative supremacy|Option B|The 1979 Constitution marked a deliberate departure from the Westminster parliamentary model by introducing an executive presidential system modeled after the United States.
11.1|Under the 1979 Presidential Constitution, which role was assigned to the executive president?|Head of State only serving ceremonial functions while a Prime Minister managed government affairs|Head of Government sharing power equally with a co-equal cabinet prime minister|Both Head of State and Head of Government combined into a single executive office|Supreme commander of the armed forces with powers to dissolve the legislature at will|Option C|Unlike the Westminster system where executive powers are split, the 1979 Constitution vested both the ceremonial role of Head of State and the executive role of Head of Government in the President.
11.1|Which constitutional doctrine was explicitly introduced to prevent the concentration of powers in a single organ during the 1979 republic?|Democratic centralism and parliamentary supremacy|The principle of separation of powers among the Executive, National Assembly, and Judiciary|Delegated legislation and bureaucratic autonomy|Unitary devolution of administrative authority|Option B|The 1979 Constitution instituted a strict separation of powers, dividing governance strictly among the Executive, the National Assembly, and the Judiciary to ensure checks and balances.
11.1|What was the primary objective of incorporating the Federal Character Principle into the 1979 Nigerian Constitution?|To centralize all federal appointments within the civil service commission of Lagos|To promote national unity and ensure balanced representation of diverse ethnic groups in public institutions|To eliminate state governments and replace them with provincial administrative zones|To enforce a strict single-party political structure across all federating units|Option B|The Federal Character Principle was designed to ensure that appointments to public service reflect the linguistic, ethnic, and geographic diversity of Nigeria, fostering inclusivity and national loyalty.
11.1|How did the 1979 Constitution attempt to curb regionalism through political party regulations?|By mandating that political parties must demonstrate a strict national spread in their membership and leadership structure|By funding only two state-approved political parties to contest national elections|By restricting political campaigns exclusively to the federal capital territory|By prohibiting regional alliances and coalitions during legislative elections|Option A|To prevent the recurrence of ethnically fractured regional parties seen in the First Republic, the 1979 Constitution required political parties to prove a broad national geographical spread.
11.1|Which organ of government under the 1979 Constitution was vested with primary lawmaking powers at the federal level?|The Federal Executive Council|The Supreme Judicial Council|The National Assembly|The National Council of States|Option C|The National Assembly, consisting of the Senate and the House of Representatives, held the exclusive constitutional authority to enact laws for the federation.
11.1|What distinguishes the executive presidential system from a parliamentary system regarding the cabinet?|Cabinet members must concurrently serve as elected members of the legislature|Cabinet members are appointed by the president from outside the legislature and are individually accountable to the executive|Cabinet decisions require a unanimous vote from all regional governors before implementation|Cabinet ministers hold absolute veto power over presidential executive orders|Option B|In an executive presidential system, ministers or commissioners are appointed by the president and do not hold seats in the legislature, adhering to the principle of separation of powers.
11.1|Why was the shift from the Westminster model deemed necessary by the constitution drafters of 1979?|The Westminster system had failed to prevent deep-seated regional polarization and instability in the First Republic|The British government demanded a constitutional rewrite as a condition for granting total economic independence|Military decrees required the immediate abolition of all democratic institutions modeled after European nations|The parliamentary system was too expensive to maintain compared to a military junta|Option A|The parliamentary system of the First Republic exacerbated ethnic divisions and instability, prompting drafters of the 1979 Constitution to look toward the American presidential model for stability.
11.1|Which institutional mechanism served as a crucial check on the executive and legislative branches under the 1979 Nigerian Constitution?|The Electoral Tribunal with powers to veto parliamentary bills|The Judiciary, wielding the power of judicial review to declare unconstitutional actions void|The Council of Traditional Rulers acting as an appellate legislative chamber|The Military High Command overseeing civil administrative policies|Option B|The Judiciary acted as the constitutional arbiter, utilizing the power of judicial review to ensure that actions of both the executive and the National Assembly conformed to the 1979 Constitution.
11.1|In the context of the 1979 Constitution, what did the requirement of a 'strict national spread' mean for presidential candidates?|Winning a simple majority of total votes cast nationwide without regional distribution requirements|Securing not only the highest number of votes nationally but also a specified minimum percentage of votes across a mandated majority of states|Obtaining unanimous endorsement from all traditional rulers in every geopolitical zone|Passing a rigorous civil service examination administered by the federal electoral commission|Option B|To ensure broad-based national legitimacy, a winning presidential candidate had to secure both popular votes nationally and a constitutional threshold of votes across a majority of the federation's states.

11.1|What fundamental institutional change characterized Nigeria's transition from the First Republic to the 1979 Presidential Constitution?|Adoption of the American Executive Presidential system combining Head of State and Head of Government roles|Retention of the British Westminster parliamentary model with a ceremonial president|Establishment of a unitary system of government abolishing the regional structures|Concentration of all legislative and judicial powers directly within the executive cabinet|Option A|The 1979 Constitution marked a deliberate departure from the Westminster system by instituting an American-style executive presidency where one individual holds both Head of State and Head of Government powers.
11.1|Which constitutional doctrine forms the bedrock of the 1979 Presidential Constitution regarding the distribution of governmental powers?|Fusion of powers through parliamentary supremacy|Separation of powers among the Executive, National Assembly, and Judiciary|Delegation of all judicial authority directly to the executive branch|Subordination of the legislature to executive decrees|Option B|The 1979 Constitution instituted a strict separation of powers, dividing responsibilities among the Executive, the National Assembly, and the Judiciary to prevent tyranny.
11.1|How does the executive presidency under the 1979 Constitution fundamentally differ from the Westminster parliamentary model?|The prime minister is accountable daily to the legislature while the president is not|The president serves as both Head of State and Head of Government unlike the split roles in a parliamentary system|The judiciary holds veto power over executive appointments in the presidential system|Ministers under the presidential system must concurrently serve as elected members of parliament|Option B|Under the Westminster system, the roles of Head of State and Head of Government are separate, whereas the 1979 Presidential Constitution merged these roles into a single executive president.
11.1|What was the primary constitutional purpose of introducing the Federal Character Principle in the 1979 Constitution?|To centralize all civil service appointments under regional governors|To ensure equitable representation of diverse ethnic groups and regions in national institutions|To establish a single-party political framework across the federation|To dissolve local government councils in favor of traditional rulers|Option B|The Federal Character Principle was designed to promote national unity and prevent ethnic dominance by ensuring public institutions fairly reflect the linguistic and geographic diversity of Nigeria.
11.1|Which requirement was strictly mandated for political parties seeking registration under the 1979 constitutional framework?|Demonstration of a strict national spread in their membership and leadership structure|Maintenance of regional offices exclusively in the northern and southern capitals|Alliance with traditional religious councils before electoral participation|Funding entirely through foreign technical grants and international donations|Option A|To prevent ethnic parochialism, political parties under the 1979 Constitution were required to exhibit a broad national spread reflecting Nigeria's diverse geographic composition.
11.1|Under the 1979 Presidential Constitution, to which body is the executive branch primarily accountable for policy implementation and budgetary approval?|The National Assembly|The Council of Traditional Rulers|The Supreme Military Council|The Judicial Service Commission|Option A|The National Assembly serves as the legislative check on the executive branch, holding oversight functions including budgetary appropriation and policy review.
11.1|What institutional mechanism under the 1979 Constitution prevents any single branch of government from exercising absolute authority?|Ministerial collective responsibility to the legislature|Checks and balances inherent in the separation of powers|Judicial appointment of the president and legislative leaders|Regional veto over federal executive decisions|Option B|The doctrine of separation of powers is reinforced by a system of checks and balances, allowing each branch to monitor and limit the actions of the others.
11.1|Which office replaced the Prime Minister of the parliamentary era when Nigeria adopted the 1979 Presidential Constitution?|Executive President|Governor-General|Sole Administrator|Head of the Interim Government|Option A|The office of the Prime Minister, typical of the Westminster system, was abolished and replaced by an Executive President who wielded comprehensive executive authority.

1.1|How are acephalous pre-colonial societies typically classified in administrative history?|As centralized empires with divine monarchs|As segmentary societies lacking a single central authority|As absolute monarchies ruled by hereditary chiefs|As militaristic city-states governed by trade guilds|Option B|Acephalous societies are non-centralized, segmentary systems where political authority is dispersed among lineages, age grades, and kinship groups rather than a single ruler.
