1.1|In the study of pre-colonial administrative systems, what does the term cephalous denote when applied to a political entity?|Headless or lacking any formal leadership hierarchy|Having a distinct political head, central authority, or institutionalized leadership core|Operating entirely on a nomadic trading economy without permanent settlements|Subordinate to an external foreign imperial power|Option B|The term cephalous literally means having a head, translating in political administration to a system with a central, institutionalized authority or monarchy.
1.1|Which administrative basis of authority relies heavily on historical continuity, ancestral roots, and generational precedents within a community?|Charismatic authority derived from temporary military conquest|Legal-rational authority based on written bureaucratic codes and statutes|Ancestral lineage and customary traditions governing social behavior and political succession|Technocratic authority based on specialized scientific expertise|Option C|Ancestral lineage serves as a core administrative basis where political rights, land tenure, and succession are determined by descent from common ancestors.
1.1|What role did customary taboos and religious rituals play in the administrative structures of pre-colonial Nigerian societies?|They served as ideological instruments that enforced social norms, maintained political stability, and legitimized authority|They were legally codified statutes enacted by elected municipal councils|They functioned solely as economic taxes collected in the form of agricultural produce|They were foreign practices introduced exclusively during the late colonial era|Option A|Customary taboos and rituals acted as powerful instruments of social control, reinforcing laws and lending sacred legitimacy to rulers and elders.
1.1|Which administrative form is best represented by institutions such as the Sokoto Caliphate and the Oyo Empire within the pre-colonial Nigerian framework?|Acephalous segmentary systems|Centralized cephalous empires and kingdoms|Stateless kinship bands without formal governance structures|Purely democratic village republics lacking any administrative stratification|Option B|The Sokoto Caliphate and Oyo Empire are prime historical instances of large-scale centralized cephalous political systems with complex administrative apparatuses.
1.1|What is the defining structural feature of an acephalous society in the study of administrative history?|The complete concentration of power in an absolute hereditary monarch and a standing cabinet|The absence of a single centralized head of state or supreme governing monarch, utilizing instead dispersed segmentary structures|The strict adherence to written constitutions and codified penal codes|The enforcement of rigid caste systems controlled by military elites|Option B|Acephalous societies are defined by the lack of a single centralized head of state, distributing administrative and judicial responsibilities across kinship groups and councils.
13.1|Which fundamental structural change was introduced by the nationwide 1976 Local Government Reform in Nigeria?|A dual-tier federated hierarchy|A uniform single-tier system of local government|A regional administrative division model|An autonomous municipal council network|Option B|The 1976 reform replaced divergent regional structures with a uniform single-tier local government system across the entire federation.
13.1|What key constitutional status was explicitly conferred upon local governments by the 1976 Local Government Reform?|Recognition as the fourth tier of government|Subordinate regional agencies of state ministries|The recognized third tier of government in the federal structure|Independent corporate entities outside federal oversight|Option C|The 1976 reform formally established local government as the third tier of government, operating below the federal and state governments.
13.1|How was the financial stability of local governments fundamentally secured following the 1976 reform?|Through direct international aid grants|Through statutory revenue allocation derived from the Federation Account|Through independent collection of international trade tariffs|Through discretionary grants issued by traditional rulers|Option B|Local governments were granted a regular, statutory share of national revenues directly from the Federation Account to ensure financial viability.
13.1|What specific administrative measure was implemented regarding traditional rulers during the 1976 Local Government Reform?|They were granted full executive chairmanship powers|They were completely abolished from governance structures|They were insulated within designated traditional advisory councils|They were appointed as regional administrative commissioners|Option C|Traditional rulers were removed from direct executive duties and insulated within advisory councils to separate traditional authority from modern governance.
13.1|What primary administrative innovation did the Dasuki Committee of 1984 recommend for local government leadership?|The appointment of military sole administrators|The establishment of executive chairmen to head local councils|The rotation of leadership among traditional chiefs|The creation of multi-member collegiate directorates|Option B|The Dasuki Committee recommended strengthening local administration by introducing executive chairmen to head local government councils.
13.1|Which major administration implemented structural changes building on the Dasuki Committee recommendations by introducing direct revenue transfers to local councils?|The Babangida administration in 1988|The Gowon military regime|The Shagari civilian administration|The Ironsi military government|Option A|The Babangida reforms of 1988 operationalized key Dasuki recommendations, including the implementation of direct revenue transfers to local governments.
13.1|What was a primary objective of insulating traditional rulers in advisory councils during the 1976 reforms?|To diminish their cultural influence permanently|To merge traditional leadership with military command structures|To depoliticize traditional authority and insulate them from partisan controversies|To transform them into judicial magistrates for local courts|Option C|Insulating traditional rulers into advisory roles protected their cultural prestige while ensuring modern local administration remained secular and professional.
13.1|Why was the 1976 local government reform considered a nationwide milestone rather than a regional initiative?|It was exclusively applied to the Northern region|It established a uniform framework applied consistently across the entire federation|It was designed solely for urban municipal centres|It was initiated by regional premiers rather than the federal military government|Option B|Unlike previous regionalized local government laws, the 1976 reform created a uniform structure implemented nationwide across all states.
13.1|What administrative deficiency prior to 1976 did the introduction of a single-tier system seek to resolve?|Excessive federal interference in municipal budgeting|Confusing multiplicity of local government structures across different regions|A complete lack of traditional leadership involvement|The absence of any form of local taxation|Option B|Different regions previously operated varying local government structures, prompting the 1976 reform to introduce a harmonized, uniform single-tier system.
13.1|In the context of the 1988 Babangida reforms, what was the significance of direct revenue transfers to local governments?|It bypassed state government bottlenecks to enhance financial autonomy and grassroots development|It allowed local governments to collect customs duties directly|It replaced local taxation with foreign loans|It centralized all local funds under military headquarters|Option A|Direct revenue transfers ensured that funds reached local governments promptly without arbitrary withholding or manipulation by state governments.
11.1|What foundational structural shift characterized the transition from the 1966 parliamentary framework to the 1979 Constitution in Nigeria?|Adoption of the French semi-presidential model with a dual executive structure|Reversion to a unitary governance system abandoning federalism entirely|Shift from the British Westminster parliamentary system to the American Executive Presidential system|Establishment of an absolute monarchy fused with regional legislative assemblies|Option C|The 1979 Constitution marked a deliberate institutional departure from the Westminster system of a split executive to the American-style presidential model.
11.1|Under the 1979 Presidential Constitution, how is the office of the Chief Executive configured in terms of state authority?|The President functions solely as Head of State while a Prime Minister manages daily administration|Executive powers are vested entirely in a collegiate council without a single dominant leader|The President combines the roles of both Head of State and Head of Government into a single office|The Head of Government is elected separately by the National Assembly while the Head of State is ceremonial|Option C|Unlike the Westminster model where ceremonial and executive duties are split, the presidential system consolidates both roles in the elected president.
11.1|Which constitutional doctrine was most explicitly introduced to prevent the concentration of powers within a single branch of government in 1979?|The principle of democratic centralism and party supremacy over state organs|The principle of separation of powers among the Executive, National Assembly, and Judiciary|The doctrine of parliamentary sovereignty superseding all judicial review|The convention of collective cabinet responsibility and legislative fusion|Option B|The 1979 Constitution explicitly distributed governance authority among distinct arms—the executive, legislature, and judiciary—to ensure checks and balances.
11.1|What was the primary objective of introducing the Federal Character Principle into the 1979 constitutional framework?|To centralize all civil service appointments under regional governors exclusively|To ensure equitable representation of diverse ethnic groups and regions in public institutions to promote national unity|To mandate strict rotational leadership between northern and southern politicians every four years|To abolish regional and state bureaucracies in favor of a monolithic administrative structure|Option B|The Federal Character Principle was designed to prevent the dominance of any single group in public governance and foster a sense of belonging across all regions.
11.1|In the context of the 1979 Constitution, what requirement was imposed on political parties to ensure they transcended narrow ethnic boundaries?|Mandatory financial backing from international organizations before registration|Requirement of a strict national spread and geographical distribution of membership and leadership|Total prohibition of any political association that had previously existed during the First Republic|Obligation to merge all regional parties into a single national mass movement|Option B|To qualify for operation and contest elections, political parties had to demonstrate a broad national spread rather than relying solely on localized or ethnic support bases.
11.1|Which organ of government under the 1979 Nigerian Constitution was vested with primary legislative powers at the federal level?|The Federal Executive Council comprising ministers appointed from all states|The National Assembly consisting of the Senate and the House of Representatives|The Supreme Court acting in consultation with the Council of State|The National Electoral Commission acting through legislative decrees|Option B|The 1979 Constitution established a bicameral National Assembly—comprising the Senate and House of Representatives—as the primary lawmaking body.
11.1|How did the 1979 Constitution alter the relationship between the executive branch and the legislature compared to the Westminster model?|Ministers were required to simultaneously retain their seats as elected members of the National Assembly|The executive branch was made completely independent of the legislature, with ministers barred from simultaneous parliamentary seats|The legislature was granted the power to dismiss the president through a simple vote of no confidence|The executive branch was stripped of any veto power over bills passed by the national legislature|Option B|Unlike the Westminster system where executive ministers are drawn from parliament, the presidential system enforces a strict separation where executive appointees cannot be sitting legislators.
11.1|What structural consequence did the adoption of the executive presidential system have on the position of the Prime Minister in Nigeria?|The office of the Prime Minister was retained with expanded executive privileges|The Prime Minister became subservient to a newly created ceremonial President|The office of the Prime Minister was formally abolished as executive powers were vested in the President|The Prime Minister was replaced by a collective executive committee of regional premiers|Option C|The shift to an executive presidency eliminated the dual executive structure, effectively abolishing the office of the Prime Minister.
11.1|Why was the incorporation of the Federal Character Principle considered a critical administrative innovation in 1979?|It resolved inter-state boundary disputes through federal judicial intervention|It served as an institutional mechanism for managing Nigeria's pluralistic diversity and ensuring bureaucratic inclusivity|It decentralized tax collection and resource control down to the local government level|It streamlined military command structures following years of military rule|Option B|It provided a constitutional safeguard to address fears of marginalization in a multi-ethnic society by institutionalizing balanced representation.
11.1|Which institutional feature best defines the system of checks and balances embedded within the 1979 Nigerian presidential framework?|The absolute immunity of executive appointees from legislative oversight or investigation|The power of the National Assembly to screen and confirm ministerial nominees and approve executive budgets|The supremacy of the judiciary over all legislative enactments and executive policy decisions without restriction|The automatic dissolution of parliament whenever the executive fails to pass a major bill|Option B|Legislative confirmation of executive appointments and budgetary oversight are core mechanisms of checks and balances in a presidential system.
12.1|Which historical commission is specifically credited with establishing four functional classes within the Nigerian civil service structure?|Udoji Commission 1974|Gorsuch Commission 1954|Ayida Panel 1997|Phillips Report 1988|Option B|The Gorsuch Commission of 1954 is historically known for establishing four distinct functional classes in the civil service to cater to different levels of skills and responsibilities.
12.1|What major administrative innovation was introduced into the Nigerian public service by the Udoji Commission of 1974?|The permanent career tenure for Permanent Secretaries|The transition of Ministers to Accounting Officers|The Unified Grading and Salary Structure (UGSS)|The total elimination of functional classes|Option C|The Udoji Commission of 1974 introduced the Unified Grading and Salary Structure (UGSS) to harmonize salaries and job evaluations across the public service.
12.1|Which modern management techniques were first recommended for adoption in the public service by the Udoji Commission?|Management by Objectives (MBO) and Planning-Programming-Budgeting System (PPBS)|Total Quality Management and Lean Six Sigma|Balanced Scorecard and Agile Project Management|Decentralized Collective Bargaining and Zero-Based Budgeting|Option A|The Udoji Commission introduced modern result-oriented management tools like Management by Objectives (MBO) and Planning-Programming-Budgeting System (PPBS) to improve efficiency.
12.1|Under the 1988 Babangida Civil Service Reform, who was designated as both the Chief Executive and the Accounting Officer of a ministry?|The Permanent Secretary|The Director-General|The Minister|The Head of Service|Option C|The 1988 reform shifted administrative control by making the Minister both the Chief Executive and the Accounting Officer, superseding the bureaucratic head.
12.1|What was a major structural change applied to the role of the Permanent Secretary by the 1988 Babangida reform?|Retitled as Director-General with a tenure tied to the political regime|Promoted to Head of the Civil Service of the Federation|Granted life tenure independent of political changes|Reassigned exclusively to judicial oversight functions|Option A|The 1988 reform renamed the Permanent Secretary position to Director-General and made it a political tenure position that changed with the government.
12.1|How did the 1988 Babangida reform affect the career mobility and scope of deployment for civil servants?|It introduced multi-ministry postings for broad experience|It restricted a professional civil servant to a single ministry throughout their career|It allowed civil servants to rotate freely between private and public sectors|It mandated foreign service postings for all senior cadres|Option B|The 1988 reform introduced single-ministry professionalization, meaning civil servants spent their entire careers within one ministry to develop deep specialized knowledge.
12.1|Which reform panel was responsible for reversing the political tenure of the bureaucratic head and restoring the permanent career status of the Permanent Secretary?|Gorsuch Commission 1954|Udoji Commission 1974|Phillips Panel 1988|Ayida Panel 1997|Option D|The Ayida Panel of 1997 recommended the reversal of the 1988 changes, restoring the title and permanent career status of the Permanent Secretary.
12.1|The Phillips Report is most commonly associated with which major administrative restructuring in Nigeria?|The 1954 Regionalization Reforms|The 1974 Structural Adjustment Program|The 1988 Babangida Civil Service Reforms|The 1997 Democratic Transition Reforms|Option C|The Phillips Report served as the foundational blueprint for the sweeping 1988 civil service reforms implemented under the Babangida administration.
12.1|What was a principal consequence of making the Minister the Accounting Officer under the 1988 reform?|The erosion of the traditional neutrality and anonymity of senior civil servants|The complete removal of political interference in ministerial spending|The enhancement of permanent career security for bureaucratic chiefs|The formal separation of political office from financial liability|Option A|Making the political Minister the accounting officer compromised the traditional anonymity and distinct separation between political leadership and administrative execution.
12.1|Which of the following commissions or panels preceded the introduction of the Unified Grading and Salary Structure (UGSS) in Nigeria?|Ayida Panel 1997|Gorsuch Commission 1954|Babangida Reform 1988|Phillips Report 1988|Option B|The Gorsuch Commission of 1954 operated long before the Udoji Commission of 1974, which subsequently introduced the UGSS.
3.1|Who served as the supreme monarch and head of the central government in the traditional administrative system of the Oyo Empire?|The Bashorun|The Alaafin of Oyo|The Aare Ona Kakanfo|The Ogboni leader|Option B|The Alaafin of Oyo held supreme political and monarchical authority at the center of the Oyo Empire's traditional administration.|
3.1|How many principal kingmaker chiefs constituted the body known as the Oyo Mesi?|Three chiefs|Five chiefs|Seven chiefs|Twelve chiefs|Option C|The Oyo Mesi was composed of seven hereditary kingmaker chiefs led by the Bashorun who held the power to select and check the Alaafin.|
3.1|Which traditional political mechanism was utilized by the Oyo Mesi to compel a tyrannical Alaafin to commit ritual suicide?|The presentation of an empty calabash or parrot eggs|A formal deposition decree issued by the military command|A judicial ruling handed down by the Ajele network|An economic blockade organized by the Ogboni society|Option A|The delivery of an empty calabash containing parrot eggs served as the constitutional symbol demanding the suicide of an overreaching or tyrannical Alaafin.|
3.1|What was the primary constitutional role of the Ogboni society within the checks and balances of the Oyo Empire?|Commanding the standing provincial armies|Serving as tax collectors in distant provinces|Mediating political conflicts between the Alaafin and the Oyo Mesi|Appointing the Aare Ona Kakanfo military commander|Option C|The Ogboni society acted as an influential earth cult and judicial body that mediated disputes to maintain constitutional equilibrium between the monarch and the Oyo Mesi.|
3.1|Who were the Ajele within the administrative framework of the Oyo Empire?|Resident monitors or provincial agents representing central authority|Elite cavalry commanders heading the Eso Ikoyi corps|Supreme military generals who faced banishment upon defeat|Chief ritual priests presiding over the presentation of parrot eggs|Option A|The Ajele functioned as central administrative agents sent to oversee provincial governance, ensure compliance, and report back to the capital.|
3.1|What distinct military responsibility defined the position of the Aare Ona Kakanfo in the Oyo Empire?|He acted as the permanent head of the civil judiciary|He served as the supreme military commander required to win all battles or die in combat|He was personally responsible for choosing the successor to the Alaafin throne|He managed internal tax collection inside the metropolitan capital|Option B|The Aare Ona Kakanfo was the supreme military commander whose martial code dictated that he must either secure victory or perish on the battlefield.|
3.1|How many elite military commanders made up the specialized corps known as the Eso Ikoyi?|Twenty commanders|Fifty commanders|Seventy commanders|One hundred commanders|Option C|The Eso Ikoyi comprised seventy elite military commanders who formed the backbone of the Oyo Empire's standing military might.|
3.1|Which specific officeholder held the leadership position among the seven kingmakers of the Oyo Mesi?|The Aare Ona Kakanfo|The Bashorun|The senior Ajele|The Onpetu of Iwo|Option B|The Bashorun headed the Oyo Mesi and played the central role in leading council deliberations and executing checks on the powers of the Alaafin.|
3.1|Which administrative organ held the primary constitutional responsibility for checking potential despotism by the supreme monarch in Oyo?|The Eso Ikoyi war council|The Ajele provincial network|The Oyo Mesi council of state|The guild of local merchants|Option C|The Oyo Mesi served as the primary legislative and check-and-balance body designed to prevent the Alaafin from exercising absolute tyranny.|
3.1|What fundamental consequence faced the Aare Ona Kakanfo if his military campaign ended in defeat?|He was required to pay a heavy fine to the royal treasury|He was demoted to the rank of a standard provincial monitor|He was expected to commit ritual suicide or die fighting on the battlefield|He was permanently exiled to the outer borders of the empire|Option C|The strict institutional code of the Aare Ona Kakanfo dictated that suffering a military defeat meant he could not return in disgrace and had to die in battle.|
4.1|Which fundamental political concept is encapsulated by the traditional Igbo maxim Igbo Enwe Eze?|Centralized monarchical absolutism|Segmentary and non-hierarchical democracy|Strict military autocracy|Feudal land ownership distribution|Option B|The phrase Igbo Enwe Eze translates to the idea that the Igbos have no king, highlighting their traditional segmentary and direct consensus democracy rather than a centralized monarchy.
4.1|What role does the Okpara play within the traditional Umunna institution?|He serves as the supreme military commander during wartime|He holds the sacred Ofo staff representing lineage truth and authority|He acts as the absolute tax collector for the entire clan|He functions as the sole judicial judge with powers of capital punishment|Option B|The Okpara is the head of the family lineage within the Umunna who holds the sacred Ofo staff, which symbolizes truth, justice, and authority.
4.1|Which governing body traditionally comprises all adult males within an Igbo village to deliberate on public affairs?|Umuada|Ndichie|Oha-na-Eze|Ozo society|Option C|Oha-na-Eze is the traditional village assembly where all adult males gather to participate in direct consensus decision-making.
4.1|What is the primary socio-political function of the Ozo or Nze title society in traditional Igbo administration?|Regulating market prices for agricultural produce|Serving as an elite military strike force|Recognizing individuals of proven integrity, wealth, and leadership|Enforcing sanitary laws throughout the community streets|Option C|The Ozo or Nze title society is a prestigious institution that embodies high moral standards, integrity, and community leadership.
4.1|Which group is primarily responsible for public works, community development, and law enforcement in traditional Igbo society?|Umuada lineage assembly|Age grades or Uke and Ogbo|Ndichie council of elders|Ozo title holders|Option B|Age grades, known as Uke or Ogbo, traditionally mobilize youth power for communal labor, public infrastructure projects, and maintaining law and order.
4.1|What distinct administrative role do the Umuada perform in traditional Igbo communities?|They act as the supreme legislative body making new laws|They function as peacebuilders and mediators within their natal lineages|They serve as tax collectors for external trade routes|They command the village defense units during external aggressions|Option B|The Umuada, consisting of daughters of the lineage, play a crucial moral and judicial role as powerful peacebuilders, mediators, and arbiters in family disputes.
4.1|How are decisions typically reached within the traditional acephalous political system of the Igbo?|Through majority vote dictated by a paramount chief|Through direct consensus among members of the community|Through decrees issued by an oracle priest|Through hereditary succession of royal edicts|Option B|Acephalous democracy in traditional Igbo society relies heavily on dialogue and direct consensus rather than majority voting or royal decrees.
4.1|What does the sacred Ofo staff primarily symbolize in the governance of the Umunna?|Agricultural fertility and abundant rainfall|Truth authority justice and ancestral connection|Military prowess and conquest over neighbors|Wealth accumulation and merchant dominance|Option B|The Ofo staff is a sacred religious and political symbol representing truth, justice, integrity, and the spiritual link to ancestors.
4.1|Who constitutes the Ndichie in the traditional administrative framework of Igbo land?|The assembly of young unmarried women|The council of elders and titled patriarchs|The group of visiting foreign traders|The guild of master blacksmiths|Option B|The Ndichie refers to the council of elders whose accumulated wisdom and experience guide community governance and conflict resolution.
4.1|Which term best describes the political structure of traditional Igbo society prior to colonial contact?|Centralized empire|Feudal dictatorship|Segmentary democracy|Absolute monarchy|Option C|Traditional Igbo society is characterized as a segmentary democracy because political power is decentralized, non-hierarchical, and distributed across various community institutions.

8.1|How did the reporting structure for traditional rulers change during the British colonial administration?|They reported directly to traditional councils and local village assemblies|They reported to District Officers and Residents rather than citizens|They reported autonomously to international judicial tribunals|They reported exclusively to indigenous cultural movements and trade unions|Option B|The colonial restructuring ensured that chiefs owed their allegiance and accountability to British administrative officers like DOs and Residents instead of their own citizens.
8.1|What effect did British colonial rule have on indigenous governance mechanisms?|Customary checks and balances were significantly eroded|Indigenous checks and balances were strengthened and codified into constitutional law|Traditional accountability frameworks became more rigid and democratic|Local governance mechanisms remained entirely untouched by British policies|Option A|The incorporation of chiefs into the colonial hierarchy disrupted indigenous systems by bypassing local customs and eroding traditional checks and balances.
8.1|Which colonial administrative officials held supervisory authority over traditional rulers in Nigeria?|Governor-Generals and Prime Ministers only|District Officers and Residents|Traditional prime ministers and council elders|Indigenous merchant guilds and youth leaders|Option B|District Officers (DOs) and Residents served as the primary colonial administrators who directly supervised and controlled the actions of traditional rulers.

8.1|The erosion of customary checks and balances under British administration was primarily driven by what factor?|The complete democratization of indigenous political structures|The subordination of chiefs to foreign colonial officers rather than local accountability|The voluntary abdication of all traditional monarchs across the region|The rapid industrialization and urbanization of rural agricultural districts|Option B|Because chiefs reported upward to colonial officers rather than downward to their people, traditional mechanisms of holding rulers accountable collapsed.

7.1|What was the primary economic motivation behind the 1914 amalgamation of the Northern and Southern Protectorates by Lord Frederick Lugard?|To finance the budget deficit of the poor North using the revenue surplus of the prosperous South and integrate railway development|To establish a unified socialist welfare system across all regions of West Africa|To prepare the indigenous populations for immediate democratic self-determination and universal suffrage|To decentralize the colonial treasury into independent municipal corporations for regional autonomy|Option A|Lugard merged the territories primarily to relieve the financially strapped Northern Protectorate using Southern customs revenues and to coordinate railway expansion.

1.1|Which of the following best describes an acephalous pre-colonial Nigerian administrative system?|A segmentary society operating without a centralized, overarching monarchical authority|A centralized empire ruled by an absolute divine monarch|A military regime controlled by a standing professional army|A colonial administrative outpost governed by foreign commissioners|Option A|Acephalous or non-centralized societies, such as the Igbo and Tiv, relied on segmentary lineages, age grades, and council systems rather than a central king.

1.1|How was political and social order primarily maintained in acephalous pre-colonial societies like the Tiv or Igbo?|Through ancestral lineages, kinship ties, age grades, and council of elders|Through royal decrees issued by an emperor and enforced by a standing army|Through centralized tax collection and a professional police force|Through international treaties negotiated with neighboring kingdoms|Option A|Lacking a central monarch, acephalous societies maintained social cohesion and order through kinship networks, lineage systems, age grades, and communal councils.

11.1|Under the 1979 Presidential Constitution, how are the roles of Head of State and Head of Government designated?|Divided between a ceremonial President and an executive Prime Minister|Vested entirely in two separate elected individuals representing different regions|Combined and vested in a single individual known as the Executive President|Assigned exclusively to the Senate President as the leader of the National Assembly|Option C|Unlike the Westminster system where executive powers are split, the 1979 Constitution combined the roles of Head of State and Head of Government in the single office of the President.
11.1|Which institutional framework forms the backbone of the checks and balances mechanism introduced by the 1979 Constitution?|Fusion of powers between the executive cabinet and the legislature|Complete subordination of the judiciary to the executive branch|Strict constitutional separation of powers among the Executive, National Assembly, and Judiciary|Centralization of all law-making and law-enforcing authority within the presidency|Option C|The 1979 Constitution institutionalized the doctrine of separation of powers, distributing governance functions independently among the Executive, National Assembly, and Judiciary.

11.1|In the context of the 1979 Constitution, what requirement was uniquely imposed on political parties seeking national recognition?|They had to maintain exclusive regional bases to safeguard minority interests|They were required to demonstrate a strict national spread in their membership and organizational structure|They had to be financially backed by international multinational corporations|They were forbidden from participating in local government elections|Option B|To avoid regional balkanization, political parties under the 1979 system were legally required to prove a broad national spread across the country to qualify for elections.

5.1|What institutional role did the Sarkin Fada perform within the traditional emirate governance structure?|Head of the palace administration and royal household|Commander-in-chief of the regional waterways and transport|Chief treasurer responsible for the public treasury and state funds|Head of the market butchers and meat trade regulation|Option A|The Sarkin Fada managed the internal affairs of the palace and oversaw the extensive retinue of royal officials and servants.
5.1|Which official was tasked with maintaining internal law, order, and police duties within the emirate administration?|Dogari|Ajiya|Sarkin Ruwa|Hakimi|Option A|The Dogari acted as the traditional police force, executing orders, maintaining public order, and carrying out enforcement duties for the authorities.
6.1|Which dynasty originally established the early administrative structure of the Benin Empire before the transition to the Oranmiyan dynasty?|The Ogiso dynasty|The Alafin dynasty|The Oba dynasty|The Uzama dynasty|Option A|The Ogiso dynasty represents the foundational era of the Benin administrative system before the transition to the Oranmiyan monarchy.
6.1|What foundational political shift occurred in the Benin administrative system with the arrival of Oranmiyan?|The establishment of the Oba monarchy|The total abolition of the traditional chieftaincy orders|The replacement of centralized governance with a democratic council|The permanent relocation of the capital to the northern savanna|Option A|Oranmiyan's arrival marked the establishment of the enduring Oba monarchy in the Benin administrative structure.
6.1|What principle governs the traditional succession to the throne of the Oba of Benin?|Primogeniture favoring the eldest son|Elective rotation among the three orders of chiefs|Appointment by the British colonial administration|Selection through a public general referendum|Option A|The political system of Benin enforces the principle of primogeniture, where the eldest son succeeds the reigning monarch.
6.1|Which prominent council functions as the traditional kingmakers in the administrative hierarchy of the Benin Empire?|Uzama N'Ihinron|Eghaevbo n'Ore|Eghaevbo n'Ogbe|Iwebo Guild|Option A|The Uzama N'Ihinron consists of seven powerful kingmakers led by the Oliha who play a central role in crowning the Oba.
6.1|Who serves as the traditional leader and head of the Uzama N'Ihinron kingmakers?|Oliha|Iyase|Ero|Eribo|Option A|Oliha is recognized as the head of the seven kingmakers comprising the Uzama N'Ihinron council.
6.1|Which group of chiefs represents the town chiefs responsible for checking the absolute powers of the Oba?|Eghaevbo n'Ore|Uzama N'Ihinron|Iwebo guild|Iweguae officials|Option A|The Eghaevbo n'Ore are the town chiefs led by the Iyase who act as a vital check on the royal power of the Oba.
6.1|Who holds the leadership position among the Eghaevbo n'Ore town chiefs in Benin administration?|Iyase|Oliha|Esogban|Ologboshere|Option A|The Iyase serves as the leader of the Eghaevbo n'Ore town chiefs and the primary voice representing civic interests against absolute monarchical overreach.
6.1|Which category of palace chiefs is specifically responsible for managing the royal regalia and treasury?|Iwebo|Ibiwe|Iweguae|Uzama|Option A|The Iwebo palace chiefs are traditionally tasked with the custody and maintenance of the Oba's royal regalia, wardrobe, and treasures.
6.1|What specific administrative portfolio falls under the jurisdiction of the Ibiwe palace chiefs?|The royal harem and domestic affairs|The imperial treasury and state finances|The executive royal guards and personal security staff|The provincial military command and defense strategy|Option A|The Ibiwe palace chiefs hold administrative charge over the royal household, including the harem and related domestic matters.
6.1|Which palace chief order is primarily responsible for attending to the personal physical needs and royal staff of the Oba?|Iweguae|Iwebo|Ibiwe|Uzama|Option A|The Iweguae palace chiefs manage the personal quarters, daily domestic support, and royal staff directly attending to the Oba.
7.1|What was the primary motive behind the 1914 amalgamation of Northern and Southern Nigeria by Lord Frederick Lugard?|Economic convenience and the integration of railway systems|To establish an immediate democratic self-governing republic|To completely eradicate traditional institutions across both regions|To unify the educational curricula of the northern and southern protectorates|Option A|Lord Frederick Lugard merged the territories primarily for economic convenience, notably to use surplus revenues from the North to subsidize the budget deficit of the South and to link the railway networks.
7.1|Which institutional pillar of the Indirect Rule system was primarily responsible for local revenue generation and expenditure management?|Native Treasury|Native Court|Native Authority|Warrant Chief Council|Option A|The Native Treasury was established under Indirect Rule to collect taxes and manage local administrative expenditures within each Native Authority.
7.1|Why did the Indirect Rule system experience profound failure in the Eastern Provinces of Nigeria?|The appointment of Warrant Chiefs disrupted egalitarian socio-political structures and sparked deep resentment|The region already possessed a well-established centralized emirate system that rejected British oversight|The British refused to introduce cash crop farming or railway lines in the eastern region|Traditional rulers in the East formed a powerful alliance with the nationalists to overthrow the governor|Option A|Unlike the North or West, the East lacked centralized authorities, leading the British to appoint artificial Warrant Chiefs whose heavy-handed taxation triggered the 1929 Aba Women's War.
7.1|The introduction of the elective principle into Nigerian politics for the first time is a defining feature of which colonial constitution?|Clifford Constitution of 1922|Richards Constitution of 1946|Macpherson Constitution of 1951|Lyttelton Constitution of 1954|Option A|The Clifford Constitution of 1922 introduced the elective principle, allowing a limited number of Africans to be elected to the legislative council, which gave rise to Herbert Macaulay's NNDP.
7.1|Which constitutional milestone officially laid the foundation for regionalism in Nigeria by dividing the country into Northern, Western, and Eastern regions?|Richards Constitution of 1946|Clifford Constitution of 1922|Macpherson Constitution of 1951|Lyttelton Constitution of 1954|Option A|The Richards Constitution of 1946 established regional assemblies for the North, West, and East, formally introducing regionalism into the Nigerian administrative framework.
7.1|The Macpherson Constitution of 1951 is best described as introducing which type of political arrangement?|Quasi-federal system|Unitary parliamentary system|Confederal confederacy model|Absolute monarchical autocracy|Option A|The Macpherson Constitution created a centralized central legislature while granting substantial legislative powers to regional assemblies, resulting in a transitional quasi-federal structure.
7.1|What major structural change was formally introduced by the Lyttelton Constitution of 1954?|Establishment of formal federalism and regional civil services|Total abolition of the regional structure in favor of a unitary state|Introduction of universal adult suffrage across the entire country|Direct appointment of all regional premiers by the British monarch|Option A|The Lyttelton Constitution of 1954 completed Nigeria's transition by establishing a formal federal system and regionalizing the civil service, judiciary, and marketing boards.
7.1|Which political party was notably formed following the introduction of the elective principle under the 1922 Clifford Constitution?|Nigerian National Democratic Party|National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons|Action Group|Northern Peoples Congress|Option A|Herbert Macaulay formed the Nigerian National Democratic Party specifically to contest the elective seats introduced by the 1922 Clifford Constitution.
7.1|The 1929 Aba Women's War was a direct consequence of resistance against administrative policies associated with which system?|Indirect Rule and taxation via Warrant Chiefs|Direct rule and the imposition of a unitary constitution|The introduction of regional civil services under federalism|The electoral rules of the 1922 legislative council|Option A|The Aba Women's War was a massive protest against direct taxation and the oppressive administrative abuses perpetrated by British-appointed Warrant Chiefs.
7.1|Which administrative mechanism was utilized by the British under Indirect Rule to adjudicate local disputes according to native law and custom?|Native Court|Legislative Council|Executive Council|Warrant Assembly|Option A|Native Courts were established to resolve local disputes and administer justice based on modified local customs, serving as a core pillar of the Native Administration system.
8.1|What primary administrative status did traditional rulers assume under British colonial rule in Nigeria?|Autonomous spiritual leaders independent of external governance|Salaried agents directly accountable to the British Crown|Elected representatives of local parliamentary systems|Independent monarchs retaining absolute sovereign powers|Option B|Under British rule, traditional rulers were integrated into the colonial apparatus as salaried agents of the Crown rather than independent sovereigns.
8.1|How did the establishment of British rule fundamentally alter the relationship between traditional rulers and their local subjects?|Chiefs began reporting primarily to British District Officers rather than their own citizens|Citizens gained direct constitutional power to depose corrupt traditional rulers|Traditional rulers shared administrative authority equally with local town assemblies|Chiefs became solely religious figures with no administrative responsibilities|Option A|The colonial administrative structure disrupted indigenous accountability, forcing chiefs to report upward to District Officers and Residents rather than downward to their citizens.
8.1|What happened to the indigenous system of checks and balances within traditional institutions during the colonial era?|They were systematically strengthened and codified into formal colonial law|They were preserved unchanged to maintain cultural continuity|They were severely eroded as traditional power became centralized under colonial oversight|They were replaced by democratic elections supervised by British Residents|Option C|Traditional checks and balances that kept rulers accountable to their communities were eroded because authority was now derived from British colonial administrators.
8.1|Which colonial administrative officials were responsible for direct supervision of traditional rulers at the local level?|Governors-General and Lieutenant-Governors|District Officers and Residents|Customs and Excise Inspectors|Colonial Legislative Council Members|Option B|District Officers and Residents were the key field administrators of the colonial government who directly oversaw traditional rulers and ensured compliance.
8.1|The transformation of traditional rulers into salaried employees of the colonial state primarily served which administrative objective?|Enhancing the traditional democratic legitimacy of indigenous African political systems|Facilitating indirect rule and efficient colonial resource extraction through local proxies|Promoting rapid industrialization and capitalist labor reforms in rural provinces|Preparing traditional institutions for immediate transition into a republic|Option B|Paying salaries turned traditional leaders into civil servants of the empire, which facilitated the implementation of the indirect rule system.
8.1|When traditional rulers began reporting to colonial authorities instead of their local populace, what was the primary political consequence?|A strengthening of indigenous constitutional monarchies across Nigeria|An increase in transparency and public participation in governance|A shift in accountability from the local citizens to the colonial masters|The complete abolition of traditional titles in all provinces|Option C|By making chiefs answerable to colonial administrators, their primary accountability shifted away from the local populace, undermining indigenous governance ethics.
8.1|In the context of British colonial administration in Nigeria, what was the defining characteristic of a chief's new position?|Elected tenure subject to popular recall by local assemblies|Bureaucratic subordination to the overarching authority of the British Crown|Absolute immunity from colonial ordinances and administrative policies|Full diplomatic status representing foreign sovereign nations|Option B|Traditional rulers lost their autonomous sovereign status and were bureaucratically subordinated to the authority of the British Crown.
8.1|Which of the following best describes the impact of British rule on the customary political structures of Nigerian societies?|Enhancement of indigenous legal systems through British legal integration|Adaptation and preservation of traditional checks and balances without interference|Subversion of indigenous accountability mechanisms to serve colonial administrative goals|Total elimination of all traditional rulers across both Northern and Southern regions|Option C|Colonial rule subverted traditional accountability structures, transforming indigenous leaders into instruments of colonial control rather than protectors of customary norms.
8.1|Why did the erosion of customary checks and balances weaken the traditional relationship between rulers and citizens?|Because citizens no longer possessed traditional mechanisms to correct or sanction high-handed behavior by chiefs|Because citizens were appointed as colonial District Officers to oversee the chiefs|Because chiefs abandoned their traditional spiritual roles entirely to study Western law|Because traditional rulers abolished all customary laws in favor of British statutes|Option A|As chiefs answered to colonial officers rather than their people, local citizens lost their traditional leverage and institutional mechanisms to check abuse of power.
8.1|The integration of traditional rulers into the colonial administration as salaried agents is a classic hallmark of which British governing policy?|Direct rule and total assimilation|Indirect rule and decentralized administration|Welfare colonialism and participatory development|Democratic federalism and constitutional devolution|Option B|The use of existing indigenous authorities as salaried agents is the defining strategy of the British indirect rule system.
